entries.summary: A muscle of facial expression that moves the scalp. It has a frontal belly in front and an occipital belly behind, joined by a flat tendon (epicranial aponeurosis, galea aponeurotica).
facts: Frontal belly: epicranial aponeurosis; occipital belly: highest nuchal line and mastoid process
Frontal belly: skin of the eyebrows and forehead; occipital belly: epicranial aponeurosis
Facial nerve (VII) – temporal branch (frontal belly) and posterior auricular nerve (occipital belly)
Supraorbital, supratrochlear, superficial temporal and occipital arteries
Raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead (surprise); pulls the scalp forwards and backwards
clinical: In peripheral facial palsy (Bell's palsy) the forehead wrinkles disappear on the same side; in a central (upper motor neuron) lesion the forehead is spared.
tus: It is continuous with the galea aponeurotica; when the galea is torn in scalp wounds, the wound gapes.
The frontal belly is supplied by the temporal branch of the facial nerve, the occipital belly by the posterior auricular nerve.

entries.summary: A ring-shaped muscle of facial expression around the eyelids and orbit that closes the eye. It has orbital, palpebral and lacrimal parts.
facts: Frontal bone (nasal part), maxilla (frontal process), medial palpebral ligament, lacrimal bone (posterior lacrimal crest)
Skin around the eye, lateral palpebral raphe
Facial nerve (VII) – temporal and zygomatic branches
Branches of the facial, superficial temporal and ophthalmic arteries
Palpebral part closes the eye gently (blinking), orbital part closes it tightly; lacrimal part helps tear flow
clinical: In facial nerve palsy the eye cannot close; it must be protected against corneal drying and ulcers.
It is the efferent limb of the corneal reflex (afferent: ophthalmic nerve).
tus: The palpebral part blinks, the orbital part screws the eye shut; the lacrimal part aids tear drainage.
When paralysed, the lower lid turns out (ectropion) and tears run down the cheek (epiphora).

entries.summary: A ring-shaped muscle of facial expression encircling the lips and forming most of their bulk. Many surrounding facial muscles blend their fibres into it.
facts: Maxilla and mandible at the level of the incisors, the modiolus at the corner of the mouth
Skin and mucosa of the lips
Facial nerve (VII) – buccal branches and marginal mandibular branch
Superior and inferior labial arteries (facial artery)
Closes, purses and protrudes the lips (whistling, kissing); takes part in speech
tus: It closes and purses the lips; it is supplied by the buccal and marginal mandibular branches of the facial nerve.

entries.summary: A thin, quadrilateral muscle of facial expression forming the deep layer of the cheek. During chewing it keeps food between the teeth.
facts: Alveolar processes of the maxilla and mandible opposite the molars, pterygomandibular raphe
Corner of the mouth (modiolus), orbicularis oris
Presses the cheek against the teeth; expels air when blowing and helps sucking (trumpeter's muscle)
sections: Relations
The parotid duct (Stensen's duct) pierces this muscle and opens into the mouth opposite the upper second molar.
tus: The parotid duct pierces buccinator opposite the upper second molar and opens into the oral vestibule.
It arises from the pterygomandibular raphe, which it shares with the superior pharyngeal constrictor.

entries.summary: The main muscle of facial expression for smiling, running from the cheekbone to the corner of the mouth.
facts: Outer surface of the zygomatic bone
Facial nerve (VII) – zygomatic and buccal branches
Draws the corner of the mouth upwards and outwards (smiling)
tus: In a genuine (Duchenne) smile, orbicularis oculi contracts together with zygomaticus major.

entries.summary: A muscle of facial expression running from below the orbit to the upper lip. By raising the upper lip it deepens the nasolabial fold.
facts: Skin and muscle of the upper lip
Facial nerve (VII) – zygomatic and buccal branches
Raises and everts the upper lip (sadness, contempt)
tus: It raises the upper lip and helps form the nasolabial fold.

entries.summary: A triangular muscle of facial expression running from the side of the lower jaw to the corner of the mouth.
facts: Facial nerve (VII) – marginal mandibular and buccal branches
Draws the corner of the mouth downwards and outwards (sadness)
clinical: If the marginal mandibular branch is injured in submandibular surgery, the corner of the mouth droops on that side.
tus: In marginal mandibular branch palsy the corner of the mouth cannot be pulled down; this branch must be protected in submandibular gland surgery.

entries.summary: A small muscle of facial expression that moves the nostrils, with a transverse part and an alar part.
facts: Maxilla (above the canine and incisor teeth)
Aponeurosis over the bridge of the nose and the alae of the nose
Narrows the nostrils (transverse part) and widens them (alar part)
tus: It has an alar part that flares the nostrils and a transverse part that narrows them; nasal flaring is seen in respiratory distress.

entries.summary: A broad, thin muscle of facial expression lying just under the skin on the front and side of the neck.
facts: Pectoral and deltoid fascia over the upper chest
Lower border of the mandible, skin of the cheek and corner of the mouth
Tenses the skin of the neck, pulls the lower lip and corner of the mouth down; expression of fear and strain
tus: The platysma lies within the superficial cervical fascia; in neck incisions it is sutured together with the skin.

entries.summary: A thick quadrilateral muscle on the ramus of the mandible that can be felt in the cheek when the teeth are clenched. Relative to its weight it is one of the strongest muscles in the body.
facts: Superficial part: anterior 2/3 of the zygomatic arch; deep part: posterior 1/3 and inner surface of the zygomatic arch
Outer surface of the ramus of the mandible, angle of the mandible and coronoid process
Masseteric artery (maxillary artery), facial artery, transverse facial artery
Elevates the mandible (closes the mouth, clenches the teeth); superficial fibres assist protrusion
clinical: Bruxism (teeth grinding) can cause hypertrophy of the muscle.
In tetanus, spasm of the muscles of mastication prevents opening of the mouth (trismus).
tus: Masseter hypertrophy is seen in bruxism; the parotid duct curves around the anterior border of masseter.
Masseter is supplied by the masseteric nerve (V3), which passes through the mandibular notch.

entries.summary: A fan-shaped muscle of mastication filling the temporal fossa.
facts: Floor of the temporal fossa and temporal fascia
Coronoid process and anterior border of the ramus of the mandible
Deep temporal arteries (maxillary artery), middle temporal artery
Elevates the mandible (anterior fibres); posterior fibres retract the mandible
clinical: Tenderness of the muscle may be found in temporomandibular joint disorders and tension-type headache.
tus: Temporalis attaches to the coronoid process; its contraction can be felt and is used in testing V3 motor function.

entries.summary: Two muscles of mastication on the inner side of the mandible, in the infratemporal fossa. The lateral pterygoid is the only muscle of mastication that opens the mouth.
facts: Lateral: upper head from the infratemporal surface of the greater wing, lower head from the outer surface of the lateral pterygoid plate; medial: inner surface of the lateral pterygoid plate, palatine bone and maxillary tuberosity
Lateral: pterygoid fovea on the neck of the mandible, articular disc and capsule; medial: inner surface of the ramus and angle of the mandible
Mandibular nerve (V3) – nerves to lateral and medial pterygoid
Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery
Lateral: protrudes the mandible and opens the mouth, moves it sideways in grinding; medial: elevates, protrudes and moves the mandible sideways
tus: The medial pterygoid and masseter wrap the angle of the mandible like a sling (pterygomasseteric sling).
The maxillary artery or buccal nerve may pass between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid.
models: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

entries.summary: The group made up of four straight (rectus) and two oblique muscles that move the eyeball, together with levator palpebrae superioris, which raises the upper eyelid.
facts: Four recti and superior oblique: common tendinous ring and its surroundings; inferior oblique: anteromedial floor of the orbit (maxilla)
Sclera; the superior oblique turns through the trochlea to the posterior superolateral quadrant of the eyeball
Oculomotor nerve (III): superior, inferior and medial rectus, inferior oblique, levator palpebrae; trochlear nerve (IV): superior oblique; abducens nerve (VI): lateral rectus
Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery

Medial rectus: adduction; lateral: abduction; superior: elevation (and intorsion); inferior: depression (and extorsion); superior oblique: depression, abduction, intorsion; inferior oblique: elevation, abduction, extorsion
sections: Memory aid
LR6SO4, the rest 3: lateral rectus is supplied by cranial nerve VI, superior oblique by IV, all the others by III.
clinical: In abducens palsy the eye turns in (esotropia) and there is double vision on looking outwards.
In oculomotor palsy the eye looks down and out, with ptosis and mydriasis.
In trochlear palsy there is double vision on looking down (going downstairs); the patient tilts the head to the healthy side.
tus: The recti arise from the common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn); the inferior oblique is the only one arising from the floor of the orbit.
Clinical testing: superior/inferior recti are tested in abduction, the obliques in adduction (H test).

entries.summary: The group of intrinsic muscles that change the shape of the tongue and extrinsic muscles that move it. The extrinsic muscles are genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus and palatoglossus.
facts: Genioglossus: superior mental spine; hyoglossus: hyoid bone (body and greater horn); styloglossus: styloid process
Underside, lateral borders and root of the tongue
Hypoglossal nerve (XII) – all tongue muscles; exception palatoglossus (vagus nerve – pharyngeal plexus)
Genioglossus protrudes the tongue; hyoglossus depresses it; styloglossus draws it up and back; intrinsic muscles change its shape
clinical: In a hypoglossal nerve lesion the protruded tongue deviates towards the paralysed side.
In loss of consciousness, if genioglossus relaxes the tongue can fall back and block the airway.
tus: The tongue muscles develop from occipital myotomes and are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (except palatoglossus).
Genioglossus paralysis (e.g. under anaesthesia) lets the tongue fall back and obstruct the airway.

entries.summary: A prominent muscle running obliquely across the side of the neck and dividing it into anterior and posterior triangles. It has two heads: sternal and clavicular.
facts: Sternal head: front of the manubrium of the sternum; clavicular head: upper surface of the medial 1/3 of the clavicle
Outer surface of the mastoid process and lateral half of the superior nuchal line
Occipital, superior thyroid and suprascapular arteries

One side: tilts the head to the same side and turns the face to the opposite side and upwards; both sides: flex the head forwards and, with the head fixed, raise the sternum as accessory muscles of respiration
clinical: Injury or fibrosis of the muscle at birth causes congenital torticollis (wry neck).
Accessory nerve injury weakens turning the head to the opposite side.
tus: SCM divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles; the accessory nerve emerges into the posterior triangle at the middle of its posterior border (near Erb's point).
In congenital muscular torticollis the head tilts towards the lesion and the face turns to the opposite side.

entries.summary: Three muscles running from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae to the first two ribs. The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass through the gap between the anterior and middle scalenes.
facts: Tubercles of the transverse processes of C2–C7
Anterior and middle: 1st rib (anterior scalene to the scalene tubercle); posterior: 2nd rib
Anterior rami of the cervical nerves (C3–C8)
Ascending cervical artery (inferior thyroid artery), transverse cervical artery
Raise the first two ribs to assist inspiration; bend the neck to the same side
sections: Relations
The phrenic nerve descends on the front of scalenus anterior. The subclavian vein passes in front of this muscle; the subclavian artery and brachial plexus pass behind it (through the scalene gap).
clinical: Compression in the scalene gap or a cervical rib can cause thoracic outlet syndrome (numbness of the arm, weak pulse).
The interscalene block is used to anaesthetise the brachial plexus for shoulder surgery.
tus: Scalenus anterior runs from the anterior tubercles of the C3–C6 transverse processes to the 1st rib; the phrenic nerve passes in front of it, the subclavian artery behind.
The scalenes raise the 1st and 2nd ribs in forced inspiration.

entries.summary: Four muscles above the hyoid bone that form the floor of the mouth: digastric, stylohyoid, mylohyoid and geniohyoid.
facts: Digastric: posterior belly from the mastoid notch, anterior belly from the digastric fossa; stylohyoid: styloid process; mylohyoid: mylohyoid line; geniohyoid: inferior mental spine
Hyoid bone (the intermediate tendon of digastric via a fibrous loop)
Anterior belly of digastric and mylohyoid: nerve to mylohyoid (V3); posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid: facial nerve (VII); geniohyoid: C1 (carried by the hypoglossal nerve)
Submental artery (facial artery), lingual artery, occipital artery
Raise the hyoid and larynx in swallowing; with the hyoid fixed they depress the mandible and open the mouth
tus: The suprahyoid muscles pull the hyoid and larynx upwards in swallowing and also help open the mouth.
Mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth (oral diaphragm); the submandibular gland wraps around its posterior border.

entries.summary: Four strap-like muscles below the hyoid bone: sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid and thyrohyoid.
facts: Sternohyoid and sternothyroid: back of the manubrium of the sternum; omohyoid (inferior belly): superior border of the scapula; thyrohyoid: oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
Ansa cervicalis (C1–C3); thyrohyoid: C1 (with the hypoglossal nerve)
Pull down and steady the hyoid and larynx during swallowing and speech
clinical: In thyroid surgery these muscles are retracted; the ansa cervicalis is preserved where possible.
tus: The intermediate tendon of omohyoid crosses in front of the internal jugular vein and is anchored to the clavicle by a fascial sling.
In thyroidectomy the infrahyoid ('strap') muscles are separated in the midline to expose the gland.

entries.la: Mm. longus colli et longus capitis
entries.summary: Deep flexor muscles of the neck lying on the front of the cervical vertebrae.
facts: Longus colli: vertebral bodies and transverse processes of C3–T3; longus capitis: transverse processes of C3–C6
Longus colli: anterior tubercle of the atlas and upper cervical vertebrae; longus capitis: basilar part of the occipital bone
Anterior rami of the cervical nerves (C1–C6)
Flex the neck and head; support the cervical lordosis
clinical: The deep neck flexors are often strained in whiplash injuries.
tus: Longus colli and capitis flex the neck; they can be strained in whiplash injury.
The 'danger space' between the prevertebral fascia and these muscles is a route by which infection can spread into the mediastinum.

entries.summary: A broad superficial muscle over the upper back and back of the neck; together with its partner it forms a diamond (hood) shape. It has upper (descending), middle (transverse) and lower (ascending) parts.
facts: Superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7–T12
Lateral 1/3 of the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula
Transverse cervical artery (superficial cervical artery), suprascapular artery, occipital artery
Upper fibres elevate the scapula (shrugging) and rotate it upwards; middle fibres retract it; lower fibres depress it and assist upward rotation
clinical: If the accessory nerve is injured in the posterior triangle during cervical lymph node biopsy, the shoulder droops and the arm cannot be raised above 90°.
The shoulder shrug test assesses the accessory nerve.
tus: Trapezius: upper fibres elevate the scapula, middle fibres retract it, lower fibres depress it; upper and lower fibres together rotate it upwards.
Its sensory (proprioceptive) fibres come from C3–C4; its motor nerve is the accessory nerve.

entries.summary: The broadest muscle in the body, covering the lower and lateral back. It forms the posterior wall of the axilla.
facts: Spinous processes of T7–L5, thoracolumbar fascia, posterior 1/3 of the iliac crest, lower 3–4 ribs, inferior angle of the scapula
Floor of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
Extends, adducts and internally rotates the arm (climbing, rowing); with the arm fixed it pulls the trunk upwards
clinical: In breast reconstruction the muscle can be used as a flap together with its vascular pedicle.
Thoracodorsal nerve injury during mastectomy weakens adduction and internal rotation of the arm.
tus: Latissimus dorsi lifts the trunk when walking on crutches.
In breast reconstruction the latissimus dorsi flap is raised on the thoracodorsal vessels.

entries.summary: Two muscles beneath trapezius running between the vertebral column and the medial border of the scapula.
facts: Minor: lower part of the nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7–T1; major: spinous processes of T2–T5
Medial border of the scapula (minor at the level of the spine, major between the spine and the inferior angle)
Dorsal scapular artery (deep branch of the transverse cervical artery)
Retract, elevate and rotate the scapula downwards; hold the scapula against the chest wall
tus: In rhomboid palsy the medial border of the scapula drifts slightly outwards; it is tested by pressing the hands on the hips.

entries.summary: A muscle on the posterolateral neck running from the upper cervical vertebrae to the superior medial angle of the scapula.
facts: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1–C4
Upper part of the medial border of the scapula (between the superior angle and the spine)
Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and C3–C4 spinal nerves
Dorsal scapular artery, transverse cervical artery
Elevates the scapula and rotates it downwards; bends the neck to the same side
clinical: Tension in this muscle is a common cause of neck pain and stiffness in desk workers.
tus: Levator scapulae is a common cause of neck pain and torticollis; it is supplied by C3–C4 and the dorsal scapular nerve.

entries.la: Mm. serrati posteriores superior et inferior
entries.summary: Thin muscles in the intermediate layer of the back that attach to the ribs; they play an accessory role in respiration.
facts: Superior: nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7–T3; inferior: spinous processes of T11–L2
Superior: upper borders of ribs 2–5; inferior: lower borders of ribs 9–12
Superior: intercostal nerves 2–5; inferior: intercostal nerves 9–11 and subcostal nerve
Superior raises the ribs, inferior pulls the ribs down (contributing to respiratory mechanics)
tus: Serratus posterior superior assists inspiration, the inferior assists expiration by pulling the ribs down; both are supplied by intercostal nerves.

entries.summary: The largest of the deep (intrinsic) back muscles, running along both sides of the vertebral column. From lateral to medial it consists of the iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis columns.
facts: Back of the sacrum, posterior iliac crest, lumbar spinous processes, sacrotuberous ligament and a common broad tendon
Iliocostalis: angles of the ribs and transverse processes of the lower cervical vertebrae; longissimus: transverse processes, ribs and mastoid process; spinalis: upper spinous processes
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior intercostal, lumbar and lateral sacral arteries
Both sides: extend the spine and head (upright posture); one side: lateral flexion to the same side; works eccentrically to control forward bending
clinical: Acute low back pain (lumbago) is often linked to spasm of this muscle group.
Strengthening this muscle group is the basis of rehabilitation in chronic low back pain.
tus: Erector spinae consists, from lateral to medial, of the iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis columns ('I Love Spine').
It controls forward bending of the trunk by eccentric contraction; spasm occurs in low back pain.

entries.summary: Deep back muscles running from the transverse processes of the vertebrae to the spinous processes above: semispinalis, multifidus and rotatores. Splenius and the short segmental muscles (interspinales, intertransversarii, levatores costarum) are also studied with this group.
facts: Transverse processes of the vertebrae and the sacrum
Spinous processes of higher vertebrae (semispinalis capitis to the occipital bone)
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior intercostal, lumbar and occipital arteries
Extend the spine and rotate it to the opposite side; provide segmental stability between vertebrae (especially multifidus)
clinical: Atrophy of lumbar multifidus is associated with chronic low back pain.
tus: Semispinalis, multifidus and rotatores belong to this group; multifidus is an important muscle for lumbar stability.
models: Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles
Ventral parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

entries.summary: Four small muscles between the base of the skull and the first two cervical vertebrae: rectus capitis posterior major and minor, obliquus capitis superior and inferior.
facts: Rectus major and obliquus inferior: spinous process of the axis; rectus minor: posterior tubercle of the atlas; obliquus superior: transverse process of the atlas
Inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone (obliquus inferior to the transverse process of the atlas)
Extend the head and rotate it to the same side; make fine postural adjustments
sections: Suboccipital triangle
The vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve lie in the floor of the triangle bounded by rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis superior and inferior.
tus: The suboccipital muscles are supplied by the suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1); C1 usually has no sensory branch.
The greater occipital nerve (posterior ramus of C2) emerges at the lower border of the suboccipital triangle; it is involved in occipital neuralgia.

entries.summary: A large fan-shaped muscle covering the upper front of the chest; it forms the anterior wall of the axilla. It has clavicular, sternocostal and abdominal parts.
facts: Clavicular part: medial half of the clavicle; sternocostal part: sternum and costal cartilages 1–6; abdominal part: aponeurosis of the external oblique
Crest of the greater tubercle of the humerus (lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus)
Pectoral branch of the thoraco-acromial artery, lateral thoracic artery, intercostal arteries
Adducts and internally rotates the arm; the clavicular part flexes, the sternocostal part extends the flexed arm; with the arm fixed it pulls the trunk up (accessory muscle of respiration)
clinical: In Poland syndrome the sternocostal part of the muscle is congenitally absent.
In heavy lifting (bench press) its tendon can tear off the humerus.
tus: Poland syndrome is the congenital absence of the sternocostal head of pectoralis major.
The anterior axillary fold is formed by pectoralis major, the posterior fold by latissimus dorsi and teres major.
models: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

entries.summary: A thin triangular muscle beneath pectoralis major. It is an important landmark because it divides the axillary artery into three parts.
facts: Outer surfaces of ribs 3–5 (near their cartilages)
Pectoral branch of the thoraco-acromial artery
Draws the scapula forwards and downwards; with the scapula fixed it raises the ribs to assist inspiration
clinical: Shortening of the muscle can compress the brachial plexus and axillary vessels beneath the coracoid process (pectoralis minor syndrome).
tus: Pectoralis minor attaches to the coracoid process; it divides the axillary lymph nodes into three levels.
The cords of the brachial plexus and the axillary artery pass beneath pectoralis minor; they may be compressed in hyperabduction.

entries.summary: A broad muscle on the side of the chest wall that attaches to the ribs like the teeth of a saw. It holds the scapula against the chest wall.
facts: Anterior (costal) surface of the medial border of the scapula, especially the inferior angle
Protracts the scapula (punching) and rotates it upwards so the arm can be raised above the head; holds the scapula on the chest wall
clinical: Injury to the long thoracic nerve during axillary lymph node dissection causes a winged scapula; when the patient pushes against a wall the medial border of the scapula lifts away clearly.
tus: Serratus anterior is known as the boxer's muscle; it draws the scapula forwards when punching.
It works with trapezius to rotate the scapula upwards; when paralysed the arm cannot be raised above 90°.

entries.la: Mm. intercostales externi, interni et intimi
entries.summary: A three-layered group of muscles filling the spaces between the ribs. The fibres of the outer layer run downwards and forwards, those of the inner layer downwards and backwards.
facts: Lower border of the rib above
Upper border of the rib below
External: raise the ribs to assist inspiration; internal and innermost: pull the ribs down in forced expiration; all strengthen the intercostal space
sections: Neurovascular bundle
The intercostal vein, artery and nerve (VAN from above down) run between internal and innermost intercostals in the costal groove on the lower border of the rib.
clinical: Pleural tap is performed just above the upper border of the lower rib to protect the neurovascular bundle.
Intercostal nerve block is used for the pain of rib fractures.
tus: External intercostal fibres run downwards and forwards ('hands in pockets'), internal intercostal fibres downwards and backwards.
External intercostals act in inspiration, the interosseous part of the internal intercostals in forced expiration.

entries.summary: The dome-shaped musculotendinous sheet separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities. It is the most important muscle of respiration; at its centre lies a trefoil-shaped tendon (central tendon).
facts: Sternal part: back of the xiphoid process; costal part: inner surfaces of costal cartilages 7–12; lumbar part: right crus (L1–L3) and left crus (L1–L2), medial and lateral arcuate ligaments
Phrenic nerve (C3–C5) – motor; the periphery receives sensory fibres from the lower intercostal nerves
Superior and inferior phrenic arteries, pericardiacophrenic artery, musculophrenic artery

On contraction the dome flattens, the vertical diameter of the thorax increases and air enters the lungs (inspiration); by raising intra-abdominal pressure it aids defecation, micturition and childbirth
sections: Openings

Caval opening (T8): inferior vena cava and branches of the right phrenic nerve; oesophageal hiatus (T10): oesophagus and vagus nerves; aortic hiatus (T12): aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein. Memory aid: 'I 8 10 eggs at 12' (IVC 8, oesophagus 10, aorta 12).
clinical: In a hiatus hernia part of the stomach passes through the oesophageal hiatus into the chest.
Irritation of the diaphragm (e.g. splenic rupture, cholecystitis) causes pain referred to the shoulder via the phrenic nerve (C3–C5 dermatomes).
High spinal cord injuries (above C3) cause diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory arrest: 'C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive'.
tus: The muscle fibres of the diaphragm arise from sternal, costal and lumbar (crural) parts and insert into the central tendon.
Bochdalek hernia (posterolateral, left) and Morgagni hernia (anterior, right) are congenital diaphragmatic hernias.

entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: A long muscle running vertically on either side of the midline of the anterior abdominal wall. Its 3–4 tendinous intersections give the 'six-pack' appearance.
facts: Superior epigastric artery (internal thoracic artery) and inferior epigastric artery (external iliac artery)
Flexes the trunk; raises intra-abdominal pressure; stabilises the pelvis against forward tilt
sections: Rectus sheath
The muscle lies in a sheath formed by the aponeuroses of the lateral abdominal muscles. The posterior layer of the sheath is absent below the arcuate line, between the umbilicus and pubis.
clinical: Separation of the two muscle bellies in the midline in pregnancy or obesity is called diastasis recti.
Rupture of the inferior epigastric artery can cause a rectus sheath haematoma.
tus: Rectus abdominis is divided by tendinous intersections ('six-pack'); these are attached to the anterior layer of the sheath.
The superior and inferior epigastric arteries anastomose in the posterior wall of the sheath.

entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: The most superficial and largest muscle of the lateral abdominal wall. Its fibres run from above and outside downwards and inwards (like hands in pockets).
facts: Linea alba, pubic tubercle and anterior half of the iliac crest; its lower border forms the inguinal ligament
Intercostal nerves (T7–T11), subcostal nerve (T12), iliohypogastric nerve
Posterior intercostal arteries, deep circumflex iliac artery
Both sides: flex the trunk and raise intra-abdominal pressure; one side: bends the trunk to the same side and rotates it to the opposite side
sections: Inguinal canal
Its aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal; the slit in the aponeurosis is the superficial inguinal ring.
clinical: Inguinal hernias develop through weak points in this region.
tus: The external oblique fibres run 'hands in pockets' (downwards, forwards and medially); acting on one side it rotates the trunk to the opposite side.
Its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament, the lacunar ligament and the superficial inguinal ring.

entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: A muscle of the lateral abdominal wall lying beneath the external oblique, most of its fibres running at right angles to it.
facts: Thoracolumbar fascia, anterior 2/3 of the iliac crest, lateral 2/3 of the inguinal ligament
Lower borders of ribs 10–12, linea alba, pubic crest and pectineal line (via the conjoint tendon)
Intercostal nerves (T7–T11), subcostal nerve, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1)
Inferior and superior epigastric arteries, deep circumflex iliac artery
Both sides: flex the trunk and raise intra-abdominal pressure; one side: bends the trunk to the same side and rotates it to the same side
sections: Cremaster muscle
In the male its lower fibres descend with the spermatic cord into the scrotum to form the cremaster muscle (genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve).
tus: The internal oblique fibres run at right angles to the external oblique; acting on one side it rotates the trunk to the same side.
The internal oblique forms the cremaster muscle and part of the conjoint tendon.

entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: The deepest muscle of the lateral abdominal wall; its fibres run horizontally and wrap the abdomen like a corset.
facts: Inner surfaces of costal cartilages 7–12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, lateral 1/3 of the inguinal ligament
Linea alba, pubic crest and pectineal line (conjoint tendon)
Intercostal nerves (T7–T11), subcostal nerve, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves
Inferior epigastric artery, deep circumflex iliac artery, posterior intercostal arteries
Compresses the abdominal viscera and raises intra-abdominal pressure; contributes to stabilising the lumbar spine (core muscle)
clinical: The TAP (transversus abdominis plane) block is injected into the plane between this muscle and the internal oblique for pain control in abdominal wall surgery.
tus: Transversus abdominis is the most important muscle for raising intra-abdominal pressure and stabilising the trunk.
In the TAP block the local anaesthetic is injected between the internal oblique and transversus.

entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: A quadrilateral muscle of the posterior abdominal wall running between the 12th rib and the hip bone.
facts: Posterior part of the iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament
Lower border of the 12th rib and transverse processes of L1–L4
Subcostal nerve (T12) and anterior rami of L1–L4
Lumbar arteries, subcostal artery, iliolumbar artery
Bends the trunk to the same side; fixes the 12th rib during inspiration; acting on both sides it extends the lumbar spine
clinical: It is one of the common muscular causes of low back pain.
tus: A muscle of the posterior abdominal wall, supplied by the subcostal nerve and the anterior rami of L1–L4.

entries.la: Diaphragma pelvis (m. levator ani, m. coccygeus)
entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: The funnel-shaped muscular layer forming the floor of the pelvic cavity. It supports the pelvic organs and contributes to continence.
facts: Levator ani: back of the pubis, tendinous arch of levator ani, ischial spine; coccygeus: ischial spine
Perineal body, anococcygeal ligament, coccyx and lower border of the sacrum
Nerve to levator ani (S3–S4), branches of the pudendal nerve
Inferior gluteal artery, internal pudendal artery, inferior vesical artery
Supports the pelvic organs and resists rises in intra-abdominal pressure; puborectalis forms the anorectal angle and maintains faecal continence
sections: Parts
Levator ani consists of the puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus. The external anal sphincter is the voluntary sphincter encircling the anal canal.
clinical: Damage to the pelvic floor muscles in childbirth can cause stress urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse; Kegel exercises strengthen these muscles.
tus: Levator ani has three parts: puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus; it arises from the tendinous arch of levator ani.
Levator ani is supplied by the S4 root and branches of the pudendal nerve; birth injury leads to stress incontinence and prolapse.

entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: A fibrous band in the midline of the anterior abdominal wall, running from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis and formed by the fusion of the aponeuroses of the lateral abdominal muscles. The umbilicus (umbilical ring) lies on it.
facts: Interlacing in the midline of the aponeuroses of the external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis
clinical: Because it is avascular, midline incisions (laparotomy) are made here.
Epigastric hernias develop through gaps in the linea alba.
tus: The linea alba is wide above the umbilicus and narrow below it; diastasis recti is separation of the rectus muscles in this region.

entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: The rolled-under lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, running between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle. It marks the boundary between the abdomen and the thigh.
facts: Muscular lacuna: iliopsoas and femoral nerve; vascular lacuna: femoral artery and vein, femoral canal (lymphatics)
Forms the floor of the inguinal canal
sections: Femoral triangle
In the triangle bounded by the inguinal ligament (above), sartorius (laterally) and adductor longus (medially) lie, from lateral to medial, the nerve, artery, vein and lymphatics (NAVeL).
clinical: Inguinal hernias are felt above the ligament, femoral hernias below it and lateral to and below the pubic tubercle.
The femoral pulse is taken just below the midpoint of the ligament.
tus: The lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's) runs from the medial end of the inguinal ligament to the pecten pubis and forms the medial border of the femoral canal.
A femoral hernia is felt below the inguinal ligament, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle; it is more common in women.

entries.summary: A strong fascial layer enclosing the deep back muscles, arranged in three layers in the lumbar region. It provides attachment for latissimus dorsi and the abdominal muscles.
facts: Anterior (in front of quadratus lumborum), middle (between quadratus lumborum and erector spinae) and posterior layer (behind erector spinae)
Latissimus dorsi, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, serratus posterior inferior
clinical: Tension and inflammation of the fascia may play a role in low back pain.
tus: The posterior layer of the thoracolumbar fascia fuses with the aponeurosis of latissimus dorsi.

entries.summary: The thick triangular muscle that forms the rounded contour of the shoulder. It has anterior (clavicular), middle (acromial) and posterior (spinal) parts.
facts: Lateral 1/3 of the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula
Posterior circumflex humeral artery, deltoid branch of the thoraco-acromial artery
Middle part: abducts the arm from 15° up to 90°; anterior part: flexion and internal rotation; posterior part: extension and external rotation
clinical: In a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus or a shoulder dislocation, axillary nerve injury paralyses deltoid and flattens the shoulder, with sensory loss over the outer shoulder (regimental badge area).
It is a common site for intramuscular injections, given 2–3 fingerbreadths below the acromion to protect the axillary nerve.
tus: The anterior fibres of deltoid flex and internally rotate, the posterior fibres extend and externally rotate.
The axillary nerve runs on the deep surface of deltoid about 5 cm below the acromion.
models: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

entries.summary: The upper member of the rotator cuff, filling the fossa above the spine of the scapula. It initiates abduction.
facts: Superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus and the joint capsule
Initiates abduction of the arm (first 15°); holds the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity
clinical: It is the most commonly torn and impinged rotator cuff muscle; its tendon is trapped under the acromion.
The 'empty can' test assesses supraspinatus; a painful arc between 60° and 120° of abduction is typical.
tus: Supraspinatus test: the 'empty can' (Jobe) test; the drop-arm test indicates a complete tear.
Calcific tendinitis is most common in the supraspinatus tendon.

entries.summary: A thick triangular muscle filling the fossa below the spine of the scapula; a member of the rotator cuff.
facts: Middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus
Rotates the arm outwards (external rotation); stabilises the head of the humerus in the glenoid
clinical: Compression of the suprascapular nerve at the spinoglenoid notch can cause wasting of infraspinatus alone (in volleyball players).
tus: Infraspinatus is supplied by the suprascapular nerve; compression at the spinoglenoid notch affects infraspinatus alone.

entries.summary: A small cylindrical muscle running from the lateral border of the scapula to the humerus; a member of the rotator cuff.
facts: Upper 2/3 of the lateral border of the scapula
Inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus
Circumflex scapular artery, posterior circumflex humeral artery
Rotates the arm outwards and adducts it slightly; stabilises the head of the humerus
sections: Spaces

Triangular and quadrangular spaces are formed between teres minor, teres major, the long head of triceps and the humerus; the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery pass through the quadrangular space.
tus: Teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve; it forms the upper boundary of the quadrangular space.

entries.summary: A large triangular muscle covering the anterior (costal) surface of the scapula; the strongest member of the rotator cuff.
facts: Rotates the arm inwards (internal rotation) and adducts it; prevents forward displacement of the head of the humerus
clinical: The lift-off (Gerber) test and belly-press test assess the integrity of subscapularis.
tus: Subscapularis is the largest and strongest muscle of the rotator cuff; it plays a major role in anterior stability.

entries.summary: A thick muscle running from the inferior angle of the scapula to the humerus; it works together with latissimus dorsi (latissimus's little helper).
facts: Posterior surface of the inferior angle of the scapula
Crest of the lesser tubercle of the humerus (medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus)
Adducts, internally rotates and extends the arm
tus: The lower border of teres major is where the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery.

entries.summary: The prominent two-headed muscle on the front of the arm. It crosses both the shoulder and the elbow joints and is the most powerful supinator of the forearm.
facts: Long head: supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula; short head: coracoid process
Radial tuberosity and, via the bicipital aponeurosis, the deep fascia of the forearm
Muscular branches of the brachial artery
Flexes the forearm and supinates it (corkscrew movement); assists flexion of the arm
clinical: When the long head tendon ruptures, the muscle belly bunches up distally (Popeye sign).
The biceps reflex tests segments C5–C6.
The brachial artery and median nerve run beneath the bicipital aponeurosis; the median cubital vein used for blood sampling lies on top of it.
tus: The biceps reflex assesses C5–C6, mainly C5.
The bicipital aponeurosis (lacertus fibrosus) covers and protects the brachial artery and median nerve.

entries.summary: A thick muscle beneath biceps, in front of the lower half of the humerus. It is the main flexor of the elbow.
facts: Lower half of the anterior surface of the humerus
Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6); its lateral part also receives fibres from the radial nerve
Flexes the forearm in every position (the 'workhorse' of elbow flexion)
clinical: After elbow fractures, ectopic ossification may develop within the muscle (myositis ossificans).
tus: Post-traumatic ossification in brachialis (myositis ossificans) may follow elbow fractures.

entries.summary: A slender muscle of the anterior compartment of the arm running from the coracoid process to the middle of the humerus. The musculocutaneous nerve pierces it.
facts: Middle of the medial surface of the shaft of the humerus
Flexes and adducts the arm; stabilises the head of the humerus
tus: Coracobrachialis flexes and adducts the arm; the musculocutaneous nerve piercing it is an important landmark.

entries.summary: A three-headed muscle occupying the entire posterior compartment of the arm. It is the main extensor of the elbow.
facts: Long head: infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula; lateral head: above the radial groove; medial head: below the radial groove
Profunda brachii artery, posterior circumflex humeral artery
Extends the forearm; the long head assists extension and adduction of the arm
clinical: The triceps reflex tests segment C7.
If the radial nerve is injured at mid-humerus, part of the medial head may be spared; in high lesions in the axilla triceps is completely paralysed.
tus: The long head of triceps arises from the infraglenoid tubercle and also crosses the shoulder.
The triceps reflex assesses segment C7.

entries.summary: A small triangular muscle on the posterolateral aspect of the elbow; it works like a continuation of triceps.
facts: Posterior surface of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
Lateral surface of the olecranon and upper part of the posterior surface of the ulna
Assists elbow extension; tenses the joint capsule and stabilises the ulna during pronation
tus: Anconeus assists elbow extension and is supplied by the radial nerve; it tenses the lateral capsule of the elbow.

entries.summary: A muscle of the upper anterior forearm running obliquely from the elbow to the middle of the radius. The median nerve passes between its two heads.
facts: Humeral head: medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon); ulnar head: coronoid process of the ulna
Middle of the lateral surface of the radius (pronator tuberosity)
Pronates the forearm; assists elbow flexion
clinical: Compression of the median nerve between the two heads (pronator teres syndrome) mimics carpal tunnel syndrome but also causes numbness of the palm.
tus: The median nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres, the ulnar artery beneath the deep (ulnar) head.
In pronator syndrome palmar sensation is also affected (unlike carpal tunnel).

entries.summary: One of the superficial muscles of the anterior forearm; at the wrist its tendon is felt just medial to the radial pulse.
facts: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon)
Flexes the wrist and deviates it radially (abduction)
sections: Landmark value
The radial pulse is taken just lateral to its tendon at the wrist.
tus: The FCR tendon is a landmark at the wrist just medial to the radial artery.

entries.summary: A forearm muscle with a thin, long tendon that is absent in about 14% of people.
facts: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon)
Assists wrist flexion; tenses the palmar aponeurosis
clinical: Its tendon is often used as a tendon graft.
At the wrist the median nerve runs just beneath and lateral to this tendon.
tus: The presence of palmaris longus is tested by touching the tips of the thumb and little finger together and flexing the wrist.

entries.summary: A superficial flexor on the anteromedial border of the forearm; one of the two anterior forearm muscles supplied by the ulnar nerve.
facts: Humeral head: medial epicondyle of the humerus; ulnar head: olecranon and posterior border of the ulna
Pisiform, hook of the hamate and base of the 5th metacarpal
Flexes the wrist and deviates it to the ulnar side (adduction)
clinical: The ulnar nerve can be compressed in the cubital tunnel between its two heads (cubital tunnel syndrome).
tus: The ulnar nerve can be compressed in the cubital tunnel between the two heads of FCU.
models: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris

entries.summary: A broad muscle forming the middle layer of the anterior compartment of the forearm. Its four tendons insert on the middle phalanges.
facts: Humero-ulnar head: medial epicondyle of the humerus and coronoid process; radial head: upper part of the anterior surface of the radius
Sides of the middle phalanges of fingers 2–5 (the tendons split to let FDP through)
Flexes the fingers at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints; assists MCP and wrist flexion
clinical: Test: with the other fingers held in extension (neutralising FDP), the PIP joint of the finger being examined is flexed.
tus: FDS flexes the proximal interphalangeal joint; in its test the other fingers are held in extension.
Before inserting on the middle phalanx, the FDS tendons split to let the FDP tendon pass (chiasma tendinum).
models: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis

entries.summary: A muscle in the deep layer of the anterior forearm that flexes the fingertips. It has a dual nerve supply.
facts: Upper 3/4 of the anterior and medial surfaces of the ulna and the interosseous membrane
Bases of the distal phalanges of fingers 2–5
Lateral half (fingers 2–3): anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve; medial half (fingers 4–5): ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
Flexes the fingertips at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints; assists flexion of all finger joints and the wrist
clinical: Rugby/jersey finger: the FDP tendon of the ring finger is avulsed from the distal phalanx.
In a high ulnar nerve lesion DIP flexion is lost in fingers 4–5.
tus: FDP is the only muscle that flexes the distal interphalangeal joint.
Jersey finger is avulsion of the FDP tendon (most often of the 4th finger) from the distal phalanx.

entries.summary: A muscle in the deep anterior layer of the forearm, in front of the radius, that flexes the tip of the thumb.
facts: Anterior surface of the radius and interosseous membrane
Base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
Flexes the interphalangeal and MCP joints of the thumb
clinical: In anterior interosseous nerve injury the thumb and index finger cannot make the 'OK' sign (pinch is impaired).
tus: FPL is the only muscle that flexes the thumb IP joint; it is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve.

entries.summary: A quadrilateral muscle running transversely between the radius and ulna at the lower end of the forearm; the principal muscle of pronation.
facts: Lower 1/4 of the anterior surface of the ulna
Lower 1/4 of the anterior surface of the radius
Pronates the forearm; holds the distal radio-ulnar joint together
tus: Pronator quadratus is the main initiator of pronation; it is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve.

entries.summary: A superficial muscle on the lateral border of the forearm. Although it is a posterior compartment muscle (radial nerve), it flexes the elbow.
facts: Upper 2/3 of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus
Base of the styloid process of the radius
Flexes the elbow when the forearm is half-pronated (as when holding a hammer); brings the forearm to the mid-position
clinical: The brachioradialis reflex tests segments C5–C6.
tus: The brachioradialis reflex assesses segment C6.
The lateral border of the cubital fossa is formed by brachioradialis, the medial border by pronator teres.

entries.tr: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
entries.la: Mm. extensores carpi radiales longus et brevis
entries.en: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
entries.summary: Two muscles on the posterolateral forearm that bend the wrist back and so strengthen the grip.
facts: Longus: lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus; brevis: lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon)
Longus: base of the 2nd metacarpal; brevis: base of the 3rd metacarpal
Longus: radial nerve; brevis: deep branch of the radial nerve (C6–C7)
Extend the wrist and deviate it radially; steady the wrist when making a fist
clinical: Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) is usually an overuse injury of the ECRB tendon at the lateral epicondyle.
tus: ECRL is supplied by the main trunk of the radial nerve, ECRB by its deep branch; ECRL is spared in PIN palsy.

entries.summary: A muscle in the middle of the posterior forearm that extends the fingers through four tendons.
facts: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon)
Extensor apparatus of fingers 2–5 (bases of the middle and distal phalanges)
Extends fingers 2–5 at the MCP, PIP and DIP joints; assists wrist extension
tus: The extensor mechanism (dorsal aponeurosis) is also the attachment of the lumbrical and interosseous muscles.
Boutonnière deformity results from rupture of the central slip; swan-neck deformity from volar plate laxity and intrinsic imbalance.

entries.summary: A superficial extensor muscle on the posteromedial border of the forearm.
facts: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus and posterior border of the ulna
Extends the wrist and deviates it to the ulnar side
tus: ECU extends the wrist and deviates it ulnarly; it is weakened in PIN palsy.
models: Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

entries.summary: A deep posterior forearm muscle wrapping the upper radius. The deep branch of the radial nerve pierces it to enter the posterior compartment.
facts: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus, radial collateral ligament, anular ligament of the radius, supinator crest of the ulna
Lateral, posterior and anterior surfaces of the upper 1/3 of the radius
Deep branch of the radial nerve (C6–C7)
Radial recurrent artery, recurrent interosseous artery
Supinates the forearm (especially with the elbow extended)
clinical: The posterior interosseous nerve can be compressed under the fibrous arch at the muscle's entrance (arcade of Frohse); finger drop develops without sensory loss.
tus: Supinator is pierced by the deep branch of the radial nerve; compression at the arcade of Frohse causes PIN syndrome.

entries.la: Mm. abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis et longus
entries.summary: Three muscles running from the deep posterior layer of the forearm to the thumb. Their tendons bound the anatomical snuffbox on the lateral side of the wrist.
facts: Posterior surfaces of the ulna, radius and interosseous membrane
APL: base of the 1st metacarpal; EPB: base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb; EPL: base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
APL abducts the thumb; EPB and EPL extend the thumb
sections: Anatomical snuffbox
It is bounded in front by the APL and EPB tendons and behind by the EPL tendon. Its floor is formed by the scaphoid and trapezium, and the radial artery runs within it.
clinical: De Quervain's tenosynovitis: inflammation of the APL and EPB tendons in the first extensor compartment (positive Finkelstein test).
After distal radius fractures the EPL tendon may rupture around Lister's tubercle.
tus: EPL tendon rupture can develop around Lister's tubercle weeks after a distal radius fracture.

entries.summary: The group forming the ball of the thumb (thenar eminence): abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and the deeply placed adductor pollicis.
facts: Flexor retinaculum, scaphoid and trapezium (adductor pollicis: 2nd–3rd metacarpals and capitate)
1st metacarpal and proximal phalanx of the thumb
Recurrent branch of the median nerve (APB, superficial head of FPB, OP); deep branch of the ulnar nerve (adductor pollicis and deep head of FPB) – C8–T1
Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery, deep palmar arch
Abduct, flex, oppose and adduct the thumb
clinical: In carpal tunnel syndrome thenar wasting and weakness of opposition develop.
In ulnar nerve injury adductor pollicis is weak; when gripping a sheet of paper the thumb IP joint flexes (Froment's sign).
tus: The thenar muscles are supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve, known as the 'million-dollar nerve'.
Ape-hand deformity results from thenar wasting and loss of opposition in median nerve injury.
models: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis

entries.summary: The group forming the swelling at the base of the little finger: abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi brevis and opponens digiti minimi.
facts: Pisiform, hook of the hamate and flexor retinaculum
Proximal phalanx of the 5th finger and 5th metacarpal
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
Deep branch of the ulnar artery
Abduct, flex and oppose the little finger
clinical: Hypothenar wasting is seen in ulnar nerve injury.
tus: The hypothenar muscles are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve, palmaris brevis by the superficial branch.
models: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

entries.summary: Four small muscles arising from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus; they are unusual in attaching to tendon rather than bone.
facts: Lateral border of the extensor apparatus of fingers 2–5
1st–2nd lumbricals: median nerve; 3rd–4th lumbricals: deep branch of the ulnar nerve
Flex the MCP joints and extend the interphalangeal joints (the 'table-holding' position)
clinical: In ulnar nerve injury a claw hand develops in fingers 4–5 (MCP hyperextension, IP flexion); ulnar paradox: with a high lesion the claw is less marked.
tus: The lumbricals are rare muscles that arise from the FDP tendons and do not attach to bone.

entries.summary: Small muscles between the metacarpal bones: four dorsal and three palmar interossei.
facts: Bases of the proximal phalanges and the extensor apparatus
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
Dorsal interossei spread the fingers (DAB – dorsal abduct); palmar interossei bring them together (PAD – palmar adduct); assist MCP flexion and IP extension
clinical: The palmar interossei are tested by gripping a sheet of paper between the fingers; they are weak in ulnar nerve lesions, and wasting is seen in the first dorsal space.
tus: There are 4 dorsal interossei and 3 (or 4) palmar interossei.
In ulnar nerve injury, wasting of the first dorsal interosseous produces a marked hollow on the back of the hand.

entries.la: M. iliopsoas (m. psoas major + m. iliacus)
entries.summary: The strongest flexor of the hip, running from the posterior abdominal wall to the thigh. It is formed by psoas major and iliacus joining in a common tendon.
facts: Psoas major: vertebral bodies and discs of T12–L4 and transverse processes of L1–L5; iliacus: iliac fossa
Psoas major: anterior rami of L1–L3; iliacus: femoral nerve (L2–L3)
Iliolumbar artery, lumbar arteries, deep circumflex iliac artery
Flexes the hip (climbing stairs, lifting the foot); with the thigh fixed it flexes the trunk (sitting up from lying)
sections: Relations

The branches of the lumbar plexus form within psoas; the femoral nerve emerges in the groove between psoas and iliacus, the obturator nerve from the medial border of psoas. Abscesses can track down the psoas sheath to the groin.
clinical: A psoas abscess (especially in tuberculous spondylitis) tracks down to the groin and thigh.
Psoas sign in appendicitis: passive extension of the right hip causes pain.
tus: Psoas major is supplied by lumbar plexus branches, iliacus by the femoral nerve.
A tuberculous psoas abscess can track along the muscle sheath to the groin and thigh.

entries.summary: The largest and heaviest muscle in the body, giving the buttock its rounded shape. In humans it is specialised for upright posture and walking.
facts: Outer surface of the ilium (behind the posterior gluteal line), back of the sacrum and coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament, thoracolumbar fascia
Iliotibial tract (most fibres) and gluteal tuberosity of the femur
Extends and externally rotates the hip; acts powerfully when rising from sitting, climbing stairs and running; stabilises the knee through the iliotibial tract
clinical: Intramuscular injections into the buttock are given in the upper outer quadrant (or ventrogluteal site) to avoid the sciatic nerve.
When the muscle is weak the trunk is thrown backwards when walking (gluteus maximus gait).
tus: Most of gluteus maximus inserts into the iliotibial tract, its deep fibres into the gluteal tuberosity.

entries.summary: A fan-shaped muscle beneath gluteus maximus on the outer surface of the ilium. It keeps the pelvis level when walking.
facts: Outer surface of the ilium (between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines)
Lateral surface of the greater trochanter
Abducts and internally rotates the hip; prevents the opposite side of the pelvis dropping when standing on one leg
clinical: In superior gluteal nerve injury the opposite side of the pelvis drops when the patient stands on one leg (positive Trendelenburg sign) and the gait waddles.
tus: Gluteus medius and minimus stop the pelvis dropping to the opposite side when standing on one leg.
Its anterior fibres internally rotate the hip.

entries.summary: The deepest and smallest of the gluteal muscles; it works together with gluteus medius.
facts: Outer surface of the ilium (between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines)
Anterior surface of the greater trochanter
Abducts and internally rotates the hip; stabilises the pelvis in walking
tus: Gluteus minimus lies beneath gluteus medius and is supplied by the same nerve (superior gluteal nerve).

entries.summary: A muscle on the upper lateral thigh lying between two layers of fascia; it acts down to the knee through the iliotibial tract.
facts: Anterior superior iliac spine and anterior part of the iliac crest
Iliotibial tubercle of the tibia (Gerdy's tubercle) via the iliotibial tract
Lateral circumflex femoral artery, superior gluteal artery
Abducts, internally rotates and flexes the hip; stabilises the extended knee
tus: TFL stabilises the extended knee through the iliotibial tract.

entries.summary: A strong fibrous band on the lateral thigh formed by a thickening of the fascia lata. Gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae insert into it.
facts: From the iliac crest to the iliotibial tubercle of the tibia
Stabilises the extended knee and the hip laterally
clinical: In runners, friction of the band over the lateral femoral epicondyle causes pain on the outer knee (iliotibial band syndrome).
tus: Iliotibial band syndrome in runners presents with pain over the lateral femoral condyle.

entries.la: M. piriformis, mm. gemelli, m. obturatorius internus et externus, m. quadratus femoris
entries.summary: A deep group of muscles behind the hip joint that rotate the thigh outwards. Piriformis is the key muscle of the region.
facts: Piriformis: front of the sacrum; obturator internus: inner surface of the obturator membrane; gemelli: ischial spine (superior) and ischial tuberosity (inferior); quadratus femoris: ischial tuberosity; obturator externus: outer surface of the obturator membrane
Greater trochanter and trochanteric fossa; quadratus femoris: intertrochanteric crest

Piriformis: S1–S2; obturator internus and gemellus superior: nerve to obturator internus (L5–S2); quadratus femoris and gemellus inferior: nerve to quadratus femoris (L4–S1); obturator externus: obturator nerve
Superior and inferior gluteal arteries, internal pudendal artery, medial circumflex femoral artery
Rotate the thigh outwards and hold the head of the femur in the acetabulum; with the hip flexed piriformis abducts
sections: Importance of piriformis

It divides the greater sciatic foramen: above it (suprapiriform) pass the superior gluteal nerve and vessels; below it (infrapiriform) the sciatic nerve, inferior gluteal nerve, pudendal nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve and inferior gluteal vessels.
clinical: Piriformis syndrome: pain radiating from the buttock down the leg due to compression of the sciatic nerve by the muscle.
tus: The short lateral rotators: piriformis, gemellus superior and inferior, obturator internus and externus, quadratus femoris.
All except obturator externus are supplied by branches of the sacral plexus; obturator externus is supplied by the obturator nerve.

entries.summary: The longest muscle in the body, crossing obliquely from lateral to medial across the front of the thigh. It is named the 'tailor's muscle' because it produces the cross-legged sitting position.
facts: Upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
Muscular branches of the femoral artery
Flexes, abducts and externally rotates the hip; flexes the knee
sections: Pes anserinus
The tendons of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus join on the medial surface of the tibia in a goose-foot shape (pes anserinus). Memory aid: 'SGT – Say Grace before Tea'.
clinical: It forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle and the anterior boundary of the adductor (Hunter's) canal; it is an important landmark for reaching the femoral vessels.
tus: Sartorius is the lateral border of the femoral triangle and the roof of the adductor canal.

entries.summary: The four-headed muscle forming most of the anterior compartment of the thigh: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and vastus intermedius. It is the only powerful extensor of the knee.
facts: Rectus femoris: anterior inferior iliac spine and upper rim of the acetabulum; vastus lateralis: greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera; vastus medialis: intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the linea aspera; vastus intermedius: anterolateral surface of the femoral shaft
Patella via the common quadriceps tendon, and the tibial tuberosity via the patellar ligament
Lateral circumflex femoral artery, femoral artery, profunda femoris artery
Extends the knee; rectus femoris also flexes the hip (the only head crossing two joints)
clinical: The patellar reflex (L3–L4) is the stretch reflex of this muscle group.
In femoral nerve injury knee extension is lost and the patient cannot climb stairs.
Vastus medialis atrophies fastest after knee surgery or immobilisation.
tus: The patellar reflex assesses segments L3–L4 (especially L4).
Quadriceps tendon rupture is more common in older people, patellar tendon rupture in younger people.

entries.la: M. adductor longus, brevis et magnus
entries.summary: The muscle group in the medial compartment of the thigh that draws the legs together. Adductor magnus is the largest of the group and has two parts.
facts: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis; hamstring part of adductor magnus: ischial tuberosity
Linea aspera of the femur; hamstring part of adductor magnus: adductor tubercle
Obturator nerve (L2–L4); hamstring part of adductor magnus: tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L4)
Adduct the thigh; assist flexion and rotation; stabilise the pelvis in walking
sections: Adductor canal
Through the opening in adductor magnus (adductor hiatus) the femoral artery and vein pass behind the knee and become the popliteal artery and vein.
clinical: In athletes a groin strain most often affects adductor longus.
tus: The adductor group (longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis, pectineus) is supplied mainly by the obturator nerve.
Groin strain most often involves adductor longus.

entries.summary: The most superficial, long and slender muscle on the medial thigh; the only muscle of the medial compartment crossing both hip and knee.
facts: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
Upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
Adducts the thigh and flexes and internally rotates the knee
clinical: The muscle is often used in plastic surgery as a functional free muscle flap.
tus: Gracilis can be used as a muscle flap and its tendon as a graft (ACL reconstruction); it is supplied by the obturator nerve.

entries.summary: A quadrilateral muscle in the floor of the femoral triangle, between iliopsoas and adductor longus.
facts: Pecten pubis (pectineal line) of the pubis
Pectineal line of the femur (below the lesser trochanter)
Femoral nerve (L2–L3), sometimes also fibres from the obturator nerve
Medial circumflex femoral artery, obturator artery
tus: Pectineus forms part of the floor of the femoral triangle.

entries.la: M. biceps femoris, m. semitendinosus, m. semimembranosus
entries.summary: Three muscles forming the posterior compartment of the thigh that extend the hip and flex the knee. Biceps femoris lies laterally, semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially.
facts: Ischial tuberosity (short head of biceps femoris: lateral lip of the linea aspera)
Biceps femoris: head of the fibula; semitendinosus: upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus); semimembranosus: posterior surface of the medial condyle of the tibia
Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2); short head of biceps femoris: common fibular part
Perforating arteries (profunda femoris artery), medial circumflex femoral artery
Extend the hip and flex the knee; biceps femoris rotates the knee outwards, semitendinosus and semimembranosus inwards
clinical: Hamstring tears are among the most common muscle injuries in sprinters.
In anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction the semitendinosus (and gracilis) tendon is often used as a graft.
tus: The hamstrings extend the hip and flex the knee; avulsion from the ischial tuberosity occurs in athletes.
Hamstring tightness can limit the straight leg raise test; it should not be confused with sciatic nerve stretch signs.

entries.summary: A two-headed hamstring muscle on the posterolateral thigh. Its tendon can be felt on the lateral side of the back of the knee.
facts: Long head: ischial tuberosity; short head: lateral lip of the linea aspera
Long head: tibial part; short head: common fibular part (L5–S2)
Flexes the knee and rotates the flexed knee outwards; the long head extends the hip
clinical: The common fibular nerve, running just medial and posterior to its tendon, can be injured in surgery on the lateral knee.
tus: Biceps femoris is a dynamic stabiliser of the lateral knee and inserts on the fibular head; the common fibular nerve runs just behind its tendon.

entries.summary: A muscle of the anterior compartment of the leg lying beside the shin bone. It lifts the foot up and turns it inwards.
facts: Lateral condyle and upper 2/3 of the lateral surface of the tibia, interosseous membrane
Medial and inferior surfaces of the medial cuneiform and base of the 1st metatarsal
Dorsiflexes (lifts) and inverts the foot; supports the medial arch
clinical: In fibular nerve injury the foot drops, and the patient lifts the knee high to avoid dragging the foot (steppage gait).
In anterior compartment syndrome there is severe pain at the front of the leg and weak dorsiflexion.
tus: Tibialis anterior palsy causes foot drop; the toes scuff the ground and the patient lifts the knee high (steppage).

entries.summary: A muscle of the anterior compartment of the leg, lateral to tibialis anterior, that lifts toes 2–5. Fibularis tertius separates from its lower part and goes to the 5th metatarsal.
facts: Lateral condyle of the tibia, upper 3/4 of the anterior surface of the fibula, interosseous membrane
Middle and distal phalanges of toes 2–5 (dorsal aponeurosis); fibularis tertius: base of the 5th metatarsal
Extends toes 2–5 and dorsiflexes the foot; fibularis tertius assists eversion
tus: EDL and fibularis tertius are in the anterior compartment; fibularis tertius dorsiflexes and everts the foot.

entries.summary: A deep muscle between tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus that lifts the big toe.
facts: Middle part of the anterior surface of the fibula and interosseous membrane
Base of the distal phalanx of the big toe
Extends the big toe and dorsiflexes the foot
clinical: Big toe extension strength is used to assess the L5 nerve root.
tus: EHL strength is the best motor test of the L5 root.

entries.summary: The superficial muscle of the lateral compartment of the leg. Its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus and under the cuboid to cross the sole of the foot.
facts: Head of the fibula and upper 2/3 of the lateral surface of the fibula
Inferior surfaces of the medial cuneiform and base of the 1st metatarsal
Everts (turns outwards) and plantarflexes the foot; supports the transverse arch
clinical: The fibular muscles and their tendons are strained in inversion ankle sprains.
tus: Fibularis longus and tibialis anterior together support the transverse arch of the foot like a 'stirrup'.

entries.summary: A muscle beneath fibularis longus whose tendon runs behind the lateral malleolus to the 5th metatarsal.
facts: Lower 2/3 of the lateral surface of the fibula
Tuberosity of the base of the 5th metatarsal
clinical: In ankle inversion its tendon can pull a fragment of bone off the base of the 5th metatarsal (avulsion fracture).
tus: The fibularis brevis tendon runs behind the lateral malleolus in front of (closer to the bone than) the longus tendon.

entries.la: M. triceps surae (m. gastrocnemius + m. soleus)
entries.summary: The powerful muscle complex that shapes the calf, made up of the two-headed gastrocnemius and the soleus beneath it. Their common tendon is the Achilles tendon (calcaneal tendon), the thickest tendon in the body.
facts: Gastrocnemius: medial head from behind the medial femoral condyle, lateral head from the lateral femoral condyle; soleus: head of the fibula, posterior surface of the fibula and soleal line of the tibia
Calcaneal tuberosity via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
Sural arteries (popliteal artery), posterior tibial artery, fibular artery
Plantarflexes the foot (rising on tiptoe, push-off in walking); gastrocnemius also assists knee flexion; soleus stops the body falling forwards when standing
sections: Muscle pump

The large venous sinuses within soleus are squeezed as the muscle contracts, pumping blood towards the heart (the 'peripheral heart'). Immobility disables this pump and raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis.
clinical: The ankle (Achilles) reflex tests segment S1.
In Achilles tendon rupture the Thompson test is positive (squeezing the calf does not move the foot).
Tennis leg: sudden tear of the medial head of gastrocnemius.
tus: Because gastrocnemius also crosses the knee, plantarflexion strength falls when the knee is bent; soleus then dominates.
The soleal line on the posterior tibia is the origin of soleus.

entries.summary: A small muscle with a short belly and one of the longest tendons in the body; it is absent in about 10% of people.
facts: Lateral supracondylar line above the lateral femoral condyle
Medial border of the calcaneal tendon or the calcaneal tuberosity
Sural branches of the popliteal artery
A weak helper of gastrocnemius in plantarflexion and knee flexion
clinical: Its tendon can be used as a graft in reconstructive surgery.
tus: Plantaris rupture can cause sudden calf pain known as 'tennis leg'.

entries.summary: A thin triangular muscle behind the knee joint, in the floor of the popliteal fossa. It is known as the 'key' that unlocks the knee.
facts: Lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle and lateral meniscus
Upper part of the posterior surface of the tibia (above the soleal line)
Medial and lateral inferior genicular arteries
Unlocks the fully extended knee (by rotating the femur laterally on the tibia); assists knee flexion
tus: The popliteus tendon passes between the lateral meniscus and the collateral ligament; it sends fibres to the posterior horn of the meniscus.

entries.summary: The deepest muscle of the posterior compartment of the leg. Its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus into the sole and is the main support of the medial arch of the foot.
facts: Interosseous membrane and adjacent posterior surfaces of the tibia and fibula
Tuberosity of the navicular, cuneiforms, cuboid and bases of metatarsals 2–4
Inverts and plantarflexes the foot; supports the medial arch
sections: Tarsal tunnel

Behind the medial malleolus, from front to back, pass: tibialis posterior tendon, flexor digitorum longus tendon, posterior tibial artery and vein, tibial nerve and flexor hallucis longus tendon ('Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry').
clinical: Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction is the commonest cause of acquired flat foot in adults.
tus: Tibialis posterior dysfunction is the commonest cause of adult acquired flat foot ('too many toes' sign).

entries.summary: A muscle in the deep layer of the posterior compartment of the leg, behind the tibia, that flexes toes 2–5.
facts: Middle part of the posterior surface of the tibia
Flexes toes 2–5; assists plantarflexion and inversion; supports the arches of the sole
tus: In the sole, the FDL tendon receives quadratus plantae and gives origin to the lumbricals.

entries.summary: A powerful muscle in the deep layer of the posterior compartment of the leg, behind the fibula, that flexes the big toe.
facts: Lower 2/3 of the posterior surface of the fibula and interosseous membrane
Base of the distal phalanx of the big toe
Flexes the big toe (final push-off in walking); assists plantarflexion; supports the medial arch
clinical: In ballet dancers its tendon can be trapped behind the talus (dancer's tendinitis).
tus: The FHL tendon runs in grooves on the posterior process of the talus and under the sustentaculum tali; tenosynovitis occurs in ballet dancers.

entries.tr: Muscles of the dorsum of the foot
entries.la: M. extensor digitorum brevis et m. extensor hallucis brevis
entries.summary: The only muscle group on the dorsum of the foot; they help the long extensors to extend the toes.
facts: EDB: long extensor tendons of toes 2–4; EHB: proximal phalanx of the big toe
Dorsalis pedis artery, lateral tarsal artery
clinical: The muscle belly, seen as a slight swelling on the dorsum of the foot, may waste in L5–S1 radiculopathy.
tus: Extensor digitorum brevis is the soft mass felt on the lateral dorsum of the foot, in front of the lateral malleolus.

entries.summary: The muscles of the sole, arranged in four layers: 1st layer abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi; 2nd layer quadratus plantae and lumbricals; 3rd layer flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis; 4th layer interossei.
facts: Calcaneus, plantar aponeurosis, tarsal and metatarsal bones
Phalanges of the toes and long flexor tendons
Medial plantar nerve (abductor hallucis, FDB, FHB, 1st lumbrical) and lateral plantar nerve (the rest) – branches of the tibial nerve (S1–S3)
Medial and lateral plantar arteries, plantar arch
Flex, spread and bring together the toes; actively support the arches and maintain balance in walking
clinical: Weakness of the plantar muscles and tightness of the plantar aponeurosis contribute to plantar fasciitis.
tus: The plantar muscles are studied in four layers; the plantar aponeurosis is the most superficial.
Plantar fasciitis typically causes heel pain worst with the first steps in the morning.
models: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

entries.summary: A two-headed muscle of mastication running horizontally in the infratemporal fossa; the only muscle of mastication that opens the mouth.
facts: Upper head: infratemporal surface and crest of the greater wing of the sphenoid; lower head: outer surface of the lateral pterygoid plate
Pterygoid fovea (neck of the mandible), articular disc and capsule (temporomandibular joint)
Nerve to lateral pterygoid (mandibular nerve, V3)
Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery
Both sides: protrude the mandible and initiate mouth opening; one side: moves the jaw to the opposite side (grinding)
clinical: In unilateral V3 injury the jaw deviates towards the paralysed side on opening (the healthy muscle pushes its condyle forwards).
tus: It is the only muscle of mastication that opens the mouth; the other three (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) close it.
Because it attaches to the articular disc it plays a role in anterior displacement of the TMJ disc.
models: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

entries.summary: A quadrilateral muscle of mastication on the inner surface of the ramus of the mandible, mirroring masseter; together they form a muscular sling around the angle of the mandible.
facts: Deep head: inner surface of the lateral pterygoid plate (pterygoid fossa) and pyramidal process of the palatine bone; superficial head: maxillary tuberosity
Inner surface of the angle of the mandible (pterygoid tuberosity)
Nerve to medial pterygoid (mandibular nerve, V3)
Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery
Elevates the mandible (closes the mouth) and assists protrusion; acting on one side it moves the jaw to the opposite side
tus: With masseter it forms the 'pterygomasseteric sling', which determines displacement of fragments in fractures of the mandibular angle.
Its nerve also supplies tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.

entries.summary: The straight muscle attached to the upper surface of the eyeball that raises the eye.
facts: Sclera, about 7.5 mm above and behind the cornea
Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery
Elevation (most effective with the eye abducted), adduction and intorsion
tus: To test pure elevation, the eye is first turned outwards (abduction) and then asked to look up.

entries.summary: The straight muscle attached to the lower surface of the eyeball that lowers the eye.
facts: Sclera, about 6.5 mm below and behind the cornea
Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery, infraorbital artery
Depression (most effective in abduction), adduction and extorsion
