clinical: In an orbital floor (blow-out) fracture the muscle can be trapped towards the maxillary sinus, causing double vision and restriction on looking up.

entries.summary: The strongest extra-ocular muscle, attached to the medial surface of the eyeball; it turns the eye towards the nose.
facts: Sclera, about 5.5 mm medial to and behind the cornea
Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery
clinical: In oculomotor nerve palsy the eye looks 'down and out' (lateral rectus and superior oblique are unopposed), with ptosis and mydriasis.
In internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion) adduction of the eye on the same side fails on lateral gaze.

entries.summary: The muscle attached to the lateral surface of the eyeball that turns the eye outwards; the only muscle supplied by the abducens nerve.
facts: Common tendinous ring (lateral part, two heads)
Sclera, about 7 mm lateral to and behind the cornea
Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery, lacrimal artery
clinical: In abducens palsy the eye turns in (esotropia) with horizontal double vision; because of its long intracranial course it is among the first cranial nerves affected by raised intracranial pressure.
tus: Mnemonic: LR6 SO4, the rest 3 (lateral rectus VI, superior oblique IV, the others III).

entries.summary: A muscle whose tendon turns through a pulley (trochlea) at the upper medial corner of the orbit to attach to the posterior superolateral quadrant of the eyeball.
facts: Body of the sphenoid (superomedial to the common tendinous ring)
Posterior superolateral quadrant of the sclera, after passing through the trochlea
Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery
Intorsion; depression (most effective with the eye adducted) and abduction
clinical: In trochlear palsy there is vertical double vision when going downstairs and reading; the patient compensates by tilting the head to the healthy side.
tus: It is the muscle for looking down and in; nerve IV is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the back of the brainstem and decussates completely.

entries.summary: A muscle that arises from the anterior floor of the orbit, passes beneath the eyeball and attaches to its posterolateral quadrant; the only extra-ocular muscle not arising from the tendinous ring.
facts: Anteromedial floor of the orbit (maxilla, lateral to the fossa for the lacrimal sac)
Posterior inferolateral quadrant of the sclera
Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery, infraorbital artery
Extorsion; elevation (most effective with the eye adducted) and abduction
tus: It produces upward and inward gaze; it is the only extra-ocular muscle arising from the floor of the orbit rather than the orbital apex.

entries.summary: The muscle that raises the upper eyelid; the smooth muscle fibres on its underside (superior tarsal muscle, Müller's muscle) have a sympathetic supply.
facts: Lesser wing of the sphenoid (above the optic canal)
Skin of the upper eyelid and superior tarsus
Oculomotor nerve (III), superior division; smooth muscle part sympathetic fibres
Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery
clinical: In oculomotor palsy there is complete ptosis; in Horner syndrome only Müller's muscle is affected, so the ptosis is mild.

entries.summary: A fan-shaped extrinsic tongue muscle that forms most of the bulk of the tongue; it protrudes the tongue.
facts: Superior mental spine (inner surface of the mandible)
Whole length of the dorsum of the tongue and body of the hyoid bone
Lingual artery (deep lingual and sublingual arteries)
Protrudes the tongue; acting on both sides it hollows the centre of the tongue
clinical: In a hypoglossal nerve lesion the protruded tongue deviates towards the side of the lesion (the healthy genioglossus pushes it that way).
Its relaxation under anaesthesia lets the tongue fall back and block the airway; the jaw-thrust manoeuvre opens it.
tus: The 'life-saving muscle': it stops the tongue falling backwards.

entries.summary: A quadrilateral extrinsic tongue muscle running from the hyoid bone to the side of the tongue; an important landmark in the submandibular region.
facts: Body and greater horn of the hyoid bone
Side and underside of the tongue
tus: The lingual artery passes deep to this muscle, while the hypoglossal nerve, lingual nerve and submandibular duct pass on its surface.

entries.summary: A muscle on the side of the neck running from the cervical vertebrae to the 1st rib; an important boundary between artery and vein.
facts: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3–C6
Scalene tubercle of the 1st rib (Lisfranc's tubercle)
Anterior rami of spinal nerves C4–C6
Ascending cervical artery, transverse cervical artery
Raises the 1st rib (forced inspiration); flexes the neck forwards and sideways and rotates it to the opposite side
clinical: In thoracic outlet syndrome the subclavian artery and brachial plexus can be compressed between the anterior and middle scalenes (scalene gap).
tus: The phrenic nerve descends on its anterior surface; the subclavian vein passes in front of the muscle, the subclavian artery and brachial plexus behind it.

entries.summary: The largest and longest of the scalenes, running from the cervical vertebrae to the upper surface of the 1st rib.
facts: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C2–C7
Upper surface of the 1st rib (behind the groove for the subclavian artery)
Anterior rami of spinal nerves C3–C8
Ascending cervical artery, transverse cervical artery
Raises the 1st rib; bends the neck to the same side
tus: The roots of the dorsal scapular nerve and long thoracic nerve pierce this muscle.

entries.summary: The smallest and deepest of the scalenes; the only scalene attached to the 2nd rib.
facts: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C4–C6
Anterior rami of spinal nerves C6–C8
Ascending cervical artery, superficial cervical artery
Raises the 2nd rib; bends the neck to the same side

entries.summary: A muscle of anterior and posterior bellies joined by an intermediate tendon; it raises the hyoid and helps open the mouth. Its two bellies develop from different pharyngeal arches.
facts: Posterior belly: mastoid notch (temporal bone); anterior belly: digastric fossa (mandible)
Intermediate tendon, attached by a fibrous loop to the body and greater horn of the hyoid bone
Posterior belly: facial nerve (VII); anterior belly: nerve to mylohyoid (mandibular nerve, V3)
Anterior belly: submental artery; posterior belly: occipital and posterior auricular arteries
Raises and steadies the hyoid bone; with the hyoid fixed it depresses the mandible (opens the mouth)
tus: The anterior belly comes from the 1st pharyngeal arch (V3), the posterior belly from the 2nd (VII); it bounds the submandibular and submental triangles.

entries.summary: A slender muscle running from the styloid process to the hyoid bone; its tendon splits to embrace the intermediate tendon of digastric.
facts: Body of the hyoid bone (at its junction with the greater horn)
Draws the hyoid bone up and back (swallowing)

entries.summary: A flat muscle whose two halves meet in the midline to form the floor of the mouth (oral diaphragm).
facts: Mylohyoid line (inner surface of the mandible)
Mylohyoid raphe and body of the hyoid bone
Nerve to mylohyoid (branch of the inferior alveolar nerve, V3)
Raises the floor of the mouth and the hyoid bone (first stage of swallowing); helps depress the mandible
clinical: The submandibular gland curls around its posterior border; infections of the floor of the mouth (Ludwig's angina) can spread above or below the muscle.

entries.summary: A short strap-like muscle lying on mylohyoid on either side of the midline.
facts: Anterior surface of the body of the hyoid bone
C1 spinal nerve fibres (carried by the hypoglossal nerve)
Draws the hyoid bone forwards and upwards; with the hyoid fixed it depresses the mandible
tus: It is the only suprahyoid muscle supplied by a cervical nerve (C1 fibres carried by XII).

entries.summary: The most superficial and most medial of the infrahyoid muscles; strap-shaped.
facts: Back of the manubrium of the sternum and medial end of the clavicle
Body of the hyoid bone (lower border)
Depresses the hyoid bone after swallowing and speech

entries.summary: A broad strap muscle deep to sternohyoid, lying just in front of the thyroid gland.
facts: Back of the manubrium of the sternum (below sternohyoid)
Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
tus: Because of this muscle's attachment, an enlarging thyroid (goitre) cannot grow upwards and extends downwards (retrosternal).

entries.summary: A short quadrilateral muscle that continues sternothyroid upwards.
facts: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
Lower border of the body and greater horn of the hyoid bone
C1 spinal nerve fibres (carried by the hypoglossal nerve)
Depresses the hyoid; with the hyoid fixed it raises the larynx (swallowing)

entries.summary: A long two-bellied muscle joined by an intermediate tendon; it subdivides the anterior and posterior triangles of the neck.
facts: Inferior belly: superior border of the scapula (near the suprascapular notch)
Superior belly: lower border of the body of the hyoid bone; the intermediate tendon is bound to the clavicle by a band of deep cervical fascia
Superior thyroid artery, transverse cervical artery
Depresses and retracts the hyoid; tenses the fascia over the internal jugular vein
tus: It divides the anterior triangle into carotid and muscular triangles, and the posterior triangle into occipital and supraclavicular triangles.

entries.summary: A three-part deep neck muscle running in front of the bodies of the cervical and upper thoracic vertebrae.
facts: Bodies of C3–T3 and transverse processes of C3–C6
Anterior tubercle of the atlas, bodies and transverse processes of C2–C6
Anterior rami of spinal nerves C2–C6
Vertebral artery, ascending cervical artery, inferior thyroid artery
Flexes the neck; acting on one side, slight rotation and lateral flexion
clinical: It is strained in whiplash injuries; a common cause of neck pain.

entries.summary: A muscle in front of and above longus colli, running from the cervical vertebrae to the base of the skull.
facts: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3–C6
Inferior surface of the basilar part of the occipital bone
Anterior rami of spinal nerves C1–C3
Ascending pharyngeal, ascending cervical and vertebral arteries

entries.summary: A short muscle between the atlas and the occipital bone, deep to longus capitis.
facts: Anterior surface of the lateral mass of the atlas
Basilar part of the occipital bone (in front of the foramen magnum)
Anterior rami of spinal nerves C1–C2
Flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint

entries.summary: A short muscle from the transverse process of the atlas to the base of the skull; it corresponds to the highest of the posterior intertransverse muscles.
facts: Jugular process of the occipital bone
Anterior rami of spinal nerves C1–C2
Bends the head to the same side (lateral flexion) and steadies it

entries.summary: A quadrilateral muscle beneath trapezius running from the thoracic vertebrae to the medial border of the scapula.
facts: Spinous processes of T2–T5 and supraspinous ligament
Medial border of the scapula (from the root of the spine to the inferior angle)
Dorsal scapular artery (deep branch of the transverse cervical artery), posterior intercostal arteries
Retracts, elevates and rotates the scapula downwards (turns the glenoid cavity down)
clinical: In a dorsal scapular nerve lesion the medial border of the scapula wings slightly away from the chest wall.

entries.summary: A small muscle just above rhomboid major, separated from it by a narrow gap.
facts: Lower part of the nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7–T1
Medial border of the scapula (level of the root of the spine)
Retracts, elevates and rotates the scapula downwards

entries.summary: A thin serrated muscle beneath the rhomboids running to the upper ribs.
facts: Lower part of the nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7–T3
Lateral to the angles of ribs 2–5
Raises the upper ribs (weakly assists inspiration)

entries.summary: A thin serrated muscle beneath latissimus dorsi running to the lower ribs.
facts: Spinous processes of T11–L2 (via the thoracolumbar fascia)
Pulls the lower ribs down and back

entries.summary: The lateral column of the erector spinae, with lumbar, thoracic and cervical parts.
facts: Iliac crest, back of the sacrum, lumbar spinous processes (common tendon) and angles of the lower ribs
Angles of the ribs and transverse processes of C4–C6
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal and lumbar arteries
Both sides: extend the spine; one side: bends it to the same side
tus: The erector spinae columns from lateral to medial: iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis ('I Love Spine').

entries.summary: The longest and thickest, middle column of the erector spinae, running from the sacrum to the skull.
facts: Common tendon (sacrum, lumbar spinous processes), thoracic and lower cervical transverse processes
Thoracic and cervical transverse processes, lower ribs and mastoid process (longissimus capitis)
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior intercostal and lumbar arteries; in the neck the occipital and deep cervical arteries
Extends the spine and head; acting on one side it bends to the same side, and longissimus capitis turns the head to the same side

entries.summary: The most medial and thinnest column of the erector spinae; it links the spinous processes together.
facts: Spinous processes of the upper lumbar and lower thoracic vertebrae
Spinous processes of the upper thoracic and cervical vertebrae (spinalis capitis: occipital bone)
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves

entries.summary: A muscle with head (capitis) and neck (colli) parts that wraps the deep back muscles like a bandage.
facts: Lower half of the nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7–T6
Splenius capitis: mastoid process and lateral 1/3 of the superior nuchal line; splenius colli: transverse processes of C1–C3
Posterior rami of the middle cervical spinal nerves
Both sides: extend the head and neck; one side: turns and tilts the head to the same side
tus: SCM turns the head to the opposite side, splenius capitis to the same side; the two act as synergists in rotation.

entries.summary: The most superficial layer of the transversospinal group, spanning 4–6 segments; its head part is the strongest extensor of the back of the neck.
facts: Transverse processes of C7–T12 (semispinalis capitis: C4–T6)
Spinous processes of higher cervical and thoracic vertebrae; semispinalis capitis: occipital bone (between superior and inferior nuchal lines)
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior intercostal, occipital and deep cervical arteries
Extends the head and spine; acting on one side it rotates to the opposite side
tus: The greater occipital nerve pierces semispinalis capitis to reach the skin of the back of the head.

entries.summary: The middle layer of the transversospinal group, made of bundles spanning 2–4 segments; it is thickest in the lumbar region.
facts: Sacrum, PSIS, lumbar mammillary processes, thoracic transverse processes, articular processes of C4–C7
Spinous processes of vertebrae 2–4 segments higher
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Stabilises the spine segment by segment; extension and rotation to the opposite side
clinical: Lumbar multifidus atrophies in chronic low back pain; it is the target muscle of stabilisation exercises.

entries.summary: The deepest layer of the transversospinal group: short muscles running from a transverse process to the lamina of the vertebra one or two levels above.
facts: Lamina and root of the spinous process of the vertebra 1–2 segments above
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Rotation and stabilisation of the spine; proprioception of spinal position
tus: They are best developed in the thoracic region; because of their dense muscle spindles they act mainly as sensory (proprioceptive) organs.

entries.summary: Small triangular muscles descending from the thoracic transverse processes to the rib below; they have short and long bundles.
facts: Between the tubercle and angle of the rib one below (short) or two below (long)
Posterior rami of spinal nerves C8–T11
Raise the ribs (assist inspiration); lateral flexion and rotation of the spine

entries.summary: A muscle running from the spine of the axis to the skull; it forms the superomedial border of the suboccipital triangle.
facts: Lateral part of the inferior nuchal line
Extends the head and rotates it to the same side

entries.summary: A small muscle from the posterior tubercle of the atlas to the occipital bone; it has a connective tissue bridge to the dura mater.
facts: Medial part of the inferior nuchal line
tus: The role of the myodural bridge between it and the dura mater in cervicogenic headache is debated.

entries.summary: A muscle from the transverse process of the atlas to the occipital bone; it forms the superolateral border of the suboccipital triangle.
facts: Occipital bone between the superior and inferior nuchal lines (lateral part)
Extends the head and bends it to the same side

entries.summary: A muscle from the spine of the axis to the transverse process of the atlas; despite its name it is the only suboccipital muscle that does not attach to the skull.
facts: Rotates the atlas (and head) to the same side (atlanto-axial rotation)
tus: The suboccipital triangle is bounded by rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis superior and inferior; it contains the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve. The greater occipital nerve emerges below the lower border of this muscle.

entries.summary: A small cylindrical muscle beneath the clavicle running to the 1st rib; it protects the vessels and nerves beneath it.
facts: Junction of the 1st rib and its cartilage
Middle 1/3 of the inferior surface of the clavicle (subclavian groove)
Steadies the clavicle and draws it down and medially
tus: In a clavicle fracture it protects the subclavian artery and vein and the brachial plexus beneath it from sharp bone fragments.

entries.summary: The most superficial muscle layer of the intercostal spaces; their fibres run downwards and forwards (like hands in pockets).
facts: Lower border of the rib above
Upper border of the rib below; in front, between the costal cartilages, they continue as the external intercostal membrane

entries.summary: The middle layer beneath the external intercostals, with fibres running downwards and backwards (at right angles to the external ones).
facts: Lower border of the rib above (outside the costal groove)
Upper border of the rib below; behind, they continue as the internal intercostal membrane
Posterior and anterior intercostal arteries, internal thoracic artery
Lower the ribs in forced expiration; the interchondral part assists inspiration

entries.summary: The innermost layer, deep to the internal intercostals, whose fibres run in the same direction as theirs.
facts: Inner surface of the rib above
Inner surface of the rib below
Act together with the internal intercostals
tus: The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs between the internal and innermost intercostals in the costal groove on the lower border of the rib, in the order vein–artery–nerve (VAN) from above down; this is why thoracentesis is done over the upper border of the rib below.

entries.summary: A thin muscle on the inner surface of the anterior chest wall, fanning out from the sternum to the costal cartilages.
facts: Back of the lower body of the sternum and xiphoid process
tus: The internal thoracic artery and vein run in front of this muscle, behind the costal cartilages.

entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: A small triangular muscle in front of the lower end of rectus abdominis; it is absent in about one person in five.
facts: Anterior surface of the pubis (pubic crest)

entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: A broad muscular sheet forming most of the pelvic floor, made of puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus.
facts: Back of the pubis, tendinous arch of levator ani (obturator fascia) and ischial spine
Perineal body, anococcygeal ligament, coccyx; puborectalis forms a sling with its partner behind the anorectal junction
Nerve to levator ani (anterior rami of S3–S4) and branches of the pudendal nerve (inferior rectal nerves)
Internal pudendal, inferior rectal and inferior gluteal arteries
Supports the pelvic organs and contracts against rises in abdominal pressure; puborectalis maintains the anorectal angle and so faecal continence
clinical: Damage to levator ani in childbirth causes pelvic organ prolapse and stress incontinence; Kegel exercises strengthen it.
tus: Puborectalis forms the anorectal angle (~90°) with its U-shaped sling; it relaxes during defecation.

entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: A triangular muscle forming the posterior part of the pelvic diaphragm; its anterior border adjoins levator ani and its posterior surface is fused with the sacrospinous ligament.
facts: Lower end of the sacrum and lateral borders of the coccyx
Anterior rami of spinal nerves S3–S4
Inferior gluteal artery, internal pudendal artery
Supports the pelvic floor; pulls the coccyx forwards after defecation and childbirth

entries.group: Muscles of the abdomen and pelvic floor
entries.summary: A voluntarily controlled ring of striated muscle around the lower 2/3 of the anal canal, with subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts.
facts: Perineal body and anococcygeal ligament (superficial part); the deep part blends with puborectalis
Around the anal canal, forming a ring with its partner
clinical: It can be damaged in 3rd- and 4th-degree perineal tears during childbirth; a pudendal nerve block relaxes the sphincter.
tus: The internal sphincter is smooth muscle under autonomic (involuntary) control; the external sphincter is striated muscle under voluntary control via the pudendal nerve.

entries.summary: A muscle on the outside of the larynx between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, with straight and oblique parts.
facts: Anterolateral surface of the arch of the cricoid cartilage
Lower border (straight part) and inferior horn (oblique part) of the thyroid cartilage
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (vagus nerve, X)
Tilts the thyroid cartilage forwards to tense the vocal folds (high pitch)
clinical: If the external branch is injured when the superior thyroid artery is tied in thyroidectomy, voice fatigue and loss of high notes result.
tus: It is the only laryngeal muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (superior laryngeal nerve, external branch).

entries.summary: The only laryngeal muscle that opens the rima glottidis, lying on the posterior lamina of the cricoid cartilage.
facts: Posterior surface of the lamina of the cricoid cartilage
Muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage
Rotates the arytenoids outwards to abduct the vocal folds (opens the rima glottidis)
clinical: In bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy the vocal folds stay in the midline and the airway is obstructed; emergency tracheotomy may be needed.
tus: It is the only muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal folds.

entries.summary: A muscle running from the upper lateral border of the cricoid to the arytenoid cartilage; the antagonist of the posterior cricoarytenoid.
facts: Upper border of the arch of the cricoid cartilage
Muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage
Rotates the arytenoids inwards to adduct the vocal folds (closes the membranous part of the rima glottidis)

entries.summary: Transverse and oblique muscles between the posterior surfaces of the two arytenoid cartilages; the oblique part continues into the aryepiglottic fold.
facts: Posterior surface of one arytenoid cartilage (oblique part: muscular process)
Posterior surface of the opposite arytenoid (oblique part: apex and aryepiglottic fold)
Bring the arytenoids together (close the intercartilaginous part of the rima glottidis); the oblique part narrows the laryngeal inlet
tus: It is the only laryngeal muscle with a bilateral nerve supply (transverse arytenoid).
models: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

entries.summary: A muscle beside the vocal fold running from the thyroid to the arytenoid cartilage; its medial fibres are distinguished as the vocalis muscle.
facts: Inner surface of the thyroid cartilage (behind its angle)
Anterolateral surface of the arytenoid cartilage and vocal process (vocalis); a part extends to the epiglottis
Relaxes and shortens the vocal folds; vocalis fine-tunes vocal fold tension

entries.summary: The thinnest of the constrictors, encircling the upper part of the pharynx.
facts: Pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe, posterior end of the mylohyoid line and side of the tongue
Pharyngeal raphe and pharyngeal tubercle (occipital bone)
Ascending pharyngeal and ascending palatine arteries
Narrows the upper pharynx in swallowing; helps the soft palate close off the nasopharynx
tus: The auditory tube and levator veli palatini pass through the gap between its upper border and the skull base.

entries.summary: A muscle that arises from the hyoid bone and fans out to encircle the middle part of the pharynx.
facts: Greater and lesser horns of the hyoid bone, stylohyoid ligament
Ascending pharyngeal artery, branches of the lingual artery
Pushes the bolus downwards in swallowing
tus: Stylopharyngeus and the glossopharyngeal nerve enter the pharynx between the middle and superior constrictors.

entries.summary: The thickest of the constrictors, made of an upper (thyropharyngeal) and a lower (cricopharyngeal) part. The cricopharyngeal part is the upper oesophageal sphincter.
facts: Thyropharyngeal part: oblique line of the thyroid cartilage; cricopharyngeal part: side of the cricoid cartilage
Pharyngeal raphe (the cricopharyngeal part forms a ring without a raphe)
Pharyngeal plexus (X); the recurrent laryngeal nerve and external laryngeal branch also supply the cricopharyngeal part
Pushes the bolus into the oesophagus; the cricopharyngeal part stays contracted at rest to prevent air swallowing
clinical: A Zenker diverticulum develops through the weak area between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal parts (Killian's triangle).

entries.summary: A long slender muscle descending from the styloid process to the pharyngeal wall; the only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
facts: Medial surface of the styloid process
Pharyngeal wall (entering between the superior and middle constrictors) and posterior border of the thyroid cartilage
Raises the pharynx and larynx and widens the pharynx in swallowing and speech
tus: It is the only muscle derived from the 3rd pharyngeal arch and the sole motor target of nerve IX.

entries.summary: A muscle descending from the soft palate to the pharyngeal wall, forming the palatopharyngeal arch (posterior pillar of the fauces).
facts: Palatine aponeurosis and posterior border of the hard palate
Lateral pharyngeal wall and posterior border of the thyroid cartilage
Raises the pharynx and larynx in swallowing; draws the two arches together to help close off the nasopharynx

entries.summary: A muscle on the posterolateral (radial) forearm running just behind brachioradialis; it steadies the wrist when making a fist.
facts: Lower 1/3 of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and lateral intermuscular septum
Dorsal surface of the base of the 2nd metacarpal
Extends and abducts the wrist (radial deviation)
tus: It receives a branch directly from the main trunk of the radial nerve before the deep branch arises; it is therefore spared in lesions in the supinator canal (posterior interosseous nerve), and the wrist deviates radially.

entries.summary: A muscle beneath the long radial extensor arising from the common extensor tendon; the commonest source of lateral epicondylitis.
facts: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon) and radial collateral ligament
Dorsal surface of the base of the 3rd metacarpal
Deep branch of the radial nerve (C7–C8)
clinical: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) is most often a tendinopathy of this muscle's origin; resisted wrist extension and middle finger extension are painful.

entries.summary: A slender muscle separated from the medial side of extensor digitorum; its tendon runs through the 5th extensor compartment.
facts: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon)
Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of the radial nerve, C7–C8)

entries.summary: A muscle in the deep posterior layer of the forearm that allows independent extension of the index finger.
facts: Lower part of the posterior surface of the ulna and interosseous membrane
Dorsal aponeurosis of the index finger (ulnar side of the extensor digitorum tendon)
tus: It is a commonly used donor tendon in tendon transfers (e.g. for EPL rupture).

entries.summary: A muscle arising from the deep posterior layer of the forearm and running to the thumb; its tendon runs with EPB in the 1st extensor compartment.
facts: Posterior surfaces of the ulna and radius and interosseous membrane
Lateral surface of the base of the 1st metacarpal
Abducts and extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint; assists wrist abduction
clinical: In De Quervain's tenosynovitis the APL and EPB tendons in the 1st extensor compartment are inflamed; Finkelstein's test is positive.
tus: With EPB it forms the lateral (radial) border of the anatomical snuffbox.

entries.summary: A short muscle just beneath APL that accompanies it.
facts: Posterior surface of the radius and interosseous membrane
Dorsal surface of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb
Extends the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joint

entries.summary: A muscle whose tendon turns around the dorsal tubercle of the radius (Lister's) to reach the distal phalanx of the thumb.
facts: Middle 1/3 of the posterior surface of the ulna and interosseous membrane
Dorsal surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
Extends the thumb at the interphalangeal and MCP joints
clinical: After a distal radius fracture (especially by friction at Lister's tubercle) the tendon may rupture ('drummer's palsy'); the tip of the thumb cannot be lifted.
tus: It is the medial (ulnar) border of the anatomical snuffbox; the floor of the snuffbox contains the scaphoid and the radial artery.

entries.summary: The most superficial and most lateral muscle of the thenar eminence.
facts: Flexor retinaculum, tubercle of the scaphoid and tubercle of the trapezium
Radial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb
Recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8–T1)
Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
Abducts the thumb at right angles to the plane of the palm
clinical: It is among the first muscles to waste in carpal tunnel syndrome; strength of palmar abduction is reduced.

entries.summary: A thenar muscle with superficial and deep heads, each supplied by a different nerve.
facts: Superficial head: flexor retinaculum and trapezium; deep head: trapezoid and capitate
Radial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb (radial sesamoid)
Superficial head: median nerve (recurrent branch); deep head: deep branch of the ulnar nerve
Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
Flexes the thumb at the MCP joint
tus: It is the thenar muscle with a dual nerve supply, so it may be partly spared in median nerve lesions.
models: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis

entries.summary: A thenar muscle deep to the short abductor, attached along the whole length of the 1st metacarpal.
facts: Flexor retinaculum and tubercle of the trapezium
Whole radial border of the 1st metacarpal
Recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8–T1)
Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
Opposes the thumb to the other fingers (opposition: flexion, abduction and medial rotation)
clinical: Superficial cuts of the recurrent branch of the median nerve (the 'million-dollar nerve') abolish opposition, producing an ape-hand appearance.

entries.summary: A triangular muscle deep in the palm with oblique and transverse heads; the thenar-region muscle supplied by the ulnar nerve.
facts: Oblique head: capitate and bases of the 2nd–3rd metacarpals; transverse head: palmar surface of the 3rd metacarpal
Ulnar side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb (ulnar sesamoid)
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
Adducts the thumb; contributes to grip strength
clinical: In ulnar nerve palsy, when the patient tries to hold paper between thumb and index finger, the thumb flexes using FPL (Froment's sign).

entries.summary: The most superficial and most medial muscle of the hypothenar eminence.
facts: Pisiform and tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the 5th finger
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
Deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery

entries.en: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand
entries.summary: A hypothenar muscle lying lateral to the abductor.
facts: Hook of the hamate and flexor retinaculum
Base of the proximal phalanx of the 5th finger
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
Deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery
Flexes the little finger at the MCP joint

entries.summary: The deepest hypothenar muscle; it attaches to the ulnar border of the 5th metacarpal.
facts: Hook of the hamate and flexor retinaculum
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
Deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery
Draws the 5th metacarpal forwards and laterally to oppose it to the thumb (cups the palm)
tus: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve winds around the hook of the hamate, passing between the abductor and the short flexor and piercing this muscle.
models: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

entries.summary: Four two-headed muscles between the metacarpals; they spread the fingers away from the axis of the middle finger.
facts: Facing surfaces of two adjacent metacarpals (two heads)
Bases of the proximal phalanges and dorsal aponeurosis: radial side of the 2nd finger, both sides of the 3rd, ulnar side of the 4th
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
Deep palmar arch, dorsal metacarpal arteries
Abduct the fingers (DAB); flex the MCP and extend the interphalangeal joints
tus: Dorsal ABduct (DAB), palmar ADduct (PAD); the 1st dorsal interosseous is the first to show wasting in ulnar nerve palsy (hollowing of the first web space).

entries.summary: Three (four in some sources) single-headed muscles on the palmar surface of the metacarpals; they bring the fingers towards the middle finger.
facts: Palmar surfaces of the 2nd, 4th and 5th metacarpals facing the middle finger (single heads)
Base of the proximal phalanx and dorsal aponeurosis of the same finger
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
Deep palmar arch, palmar metacarpal arteries
Adduct the fingers (PAD); MCP flexion and IP extension
clinical: In ulnar nerve palsy the card test (holding paper between the fingers) is weak; loss of the interossei contributes to the claw hand.

entries.summary: A long spindle-shaped muscle arising beside the lumbar vertebrae and passing under the inguinal ligament into the thigh; with iliacus it forms iliopsoas.
facts: Bodies of T12–L4 and the intervening discs, transverse processes of L1–L5
Anterior rami of spinal nerves L1–L3
The strongest flexor of the hip; with the thigh fixed it flexes the trunk and bends the lumbar spine laterally
clinical: A psoas abscess (e.g. spinal tuberculosis) tracks down the muscle sheath to the groin and causes a swelling in the upper front of the thigh.
Psoas sign in appendicitis: passive extension of the right hip is painful.
tus: The lumbar plexus forms within the muscle; the femoral nerve emerges from its lateral border, the obturator nerve from its medial border, the genitofemoral nerve from its anterior surface.

entries.summary: A fan-shaped muscle filling the iliac fossa; its tendon joins that of psoas major.
facts: Upper 2/3 of the iliac fossa, inner lip of the iliac crest, ala of the sacrum and area around the AIIS
Lesser trochanter (with the psoas major tendon)
Iliac branch of the iliolumbar artery, deep circumflex iliac artery
Flexes the hip; tilts the pelvis forwards

entries.summary: A muscle that passes through the greater sciatic foramen into the gluteal region; the key landmark of that region.
facts: Anterior surface of the sacrum (level of S2–S4) and margin of the greater sciatic notch
Upper border of the greater trochanter
Rotates the hip outwards; abducts the flexed hip; holds the head of the femur in the acetabulum
clinical: In piriformis syndrome the sciatic nerve is compressed under the muscle, causing buttock pain and sciatica.
tus: It divides the greater sciatic foramen into suprapiriform (superior gluteal artery, vein and nerve) and infrapiriform (sciatic nerve, inferior gluteal vessels and nerve, pudendal nerve, internal pudendal artery, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve) openings.

entries.summary: A muscle arising on the inner side wall of the pelvis whose tendon turns out through the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the trochanter.
facts: Inner surface of the obturator membrane and the surrounding bone of the obturator foramen
Medial surface of the greater trochanter (above the trochanteric fossa)
Rotates the hip outwards; abducts the flexed hip
tus: As its tendon leaves through the lesser sciatic foramen it turns like a pulley over the lesser sciatic notch; its fascia forms the wall of the pudendal (Alcock's) canal.

entries.summary: A small muscle accompanying the upper border of the obturator internus tendon.
facts: Medial surface of the greater trochanter, with the obturator internus tendon

entries.summary: A small muscle accompanying the lower border of the obturator internus tendon.
facts: Upper part of the ischial tuberosity
Medial surface of the greater trochanter, with the obturator internus tendon
Inferior gluteal artery, medial circumflex femoral artery
tus: The gemelli have different nerves: the superior gemellus is supplied by the nerve to obturator internus, the inferior by the nerve to quadratus femoris.

entries.summary: A quadrilateral muscle running horizontally between the ischial tuberosity and the femur.
facts: Lateral border of the ischial tuberosity
Quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest
A strong lateral rotator of the hip
tus: The medial circumflex femoral artery runs deep to this muscle; as the main supply of the femoral head it must be protected in posterior surgical approaches.

entries.summary: A muscle arising from the outer surface of the obturator membrane and passing under the femoral neck to the trochanteric fossa.
facts: Outer surface of the obturator membrane and the surrounding bone of the obturator foramen
Posterior branch of the obturator nerve (L3–L4)
Obturator artery, medial circumflex femoral artery
Rotates the hip outwards; steadies the head of the femur
tus: It is the only short lateral rotator supplied by the obturator nerve; anatomically it is counted among the adductors.

entries.summary: The central superficial head of quadriceps; the only quadriceps head that crosses both the hip and the knee.
facts: Straight head: anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS); reflected head: upper rim of the acetabulum (supra-acetabular groove)
Tibial tuberosity via the patella and patellar ligament
Extends the knee and flexes the hip
clinical: In adolescent athletes it can cause an AIIS avulsion fracture; contracting during hip flexion and knee extension at once makes it prone to strains.

entries.summary: The largest head of quadriceps, covering the lateral surface of the thigh.
facts: Upper intertrochanteric line, greater trochanter, gluteal tuberosity and lateral lip of the linea aspera
Lateral border of the patella via the quadriceps tendon, and the tibial tuberosity via the patellar ligament
tus: It is the preferred site for intramuscular injection in children (lateral surface of the middle third of the thigh).

entries.summary: The teardrop-shaped head of quadriceps prominent on the lower inner thigh; its lower oblique fibres (VMO) pull the patella medially.
facts: Lower intertrochanteric line, medial lip of the linea aspera and medial intermuscular septum
Medial border of the patella and quadriceps tendon; tibial tuberosity via the patellar ligament
Extends the knee; its oblique fibres stop the patella sliding laterally
clinical: VMO weakness predisposes to patellofemoral pain and lateral dislocation of the patella; it is the first to waste after knee surgery.

entries.summary: The deep head of quadriceps beneath rectus femoris, attached to the anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft.
facts: Upper 2/3 of the anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft
Deep layer of the quadriceps tendon; patella and tibial tuberosity
Lateral circumflex femoral artery, profunda femoris artery
tus: The articularis genus beneath it pulls the suprapatellar bursa upwards during knee extension so it is not pinched.

entries.summary: The most anterior and superficial flat muscle of the adductor group; it forms the medial border of the femoral triangle.
facts: Body of the pubis (below the pubic crest)
Middle 1/3 of the linea aspera (medial lip)
Anterior branch of the obturator nerve (L2–L4)
Adducts the hip; assists flexion and internal rotation
clinical: It is the adductor most often injured in groin strains; common in footballers.
tus: Femoral triangle: inguinal ligament (above), sartorius (lateral), adductor longus (medial border).

entries.summary: A short triangular muscle deep to adductor longus; the branches of the obturator nerve pass in front of and behind it.
facts: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
Pectineal line and upper linea aspera
tus: The anterior branch of the obturator nerve passes in front of the muscle, the posterior branch behind it.

entries.summary: The largest of the adductors, with an adductor part and a hamstring (ischiocondylar) part supplied by two different nerves.
facts: Adductor part: inferior pubic ramus and ischial ramus; hamstring part: ischial tuberosity
Adductor part: gluteal tuberosity and linea aspera; hamstring part: adductor tubercle (femur)
Adductor part: obturator nerve (L2–L4); hamstring part: tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L4)
Profunda femoris artery (perforating arteries), obturator artery
Adducts the hip; the adductor part flexes, the hamstring part extends
tus: Through the adductor hiatus between its two insertions the femoral artery and vein pass into the popliteal fossa and become the popliteal artery and vein.

entries.summary: A hamstring muscle on the posteromedial thigh whose lower half becomes a long tendon.
facts: Ischial tuberosity (common tendon with the long head of biceps femoris)
Upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
Perforating arteries of the profunda femoris, medial circumflex femoral artery
Flexes the knee and extends the hip; rotates the leg inwards when the knee is bent
tus: The pes anserinus is formed by sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus ('SGT'); its tendon is used as a graft in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

entries.summary: A hamstring muscle deep to semitendinosus whose upper part is flat like a membrane.
facts: Upper lateral part of the ischial tuberosity
Posterior surface of the medial condyle of the tibia; its expansions form the oblique popliteal ligament
Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
Perforating arteries of the profunda femoris, branches of the popliteal artery
Flexes the knee and extends the hip; rotates the leg inwards when the knee is bent
clinical: Enlargement of the bursa between the medial head of gastrocnemius and semimembranosus is a Baker's (popliteal) cyst.

entries.summary: A muscle separated from the lower lateral part of extensor digitorum longus, running to the 5th metatarsal; it is absent in some people.
facts: Lower 1/3 of the anterior surface of the fibula and interosseous membrane
Dorsal surface of the base of the 5th metatarsal
tus: It is the only evertor in the anterior compartment; the other evertors (fibularis longus and brevis) are in the lateral compartment.

entries.summary: The superficial two-headed muscle of the calf; it crosses both the knee and the ankle.
facts: Medial head: upper posterior part of the medial femoral condyle; lateral head: lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle
Calcaneal tuberosity via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
Plantarflexes the foot (running, jumping); flexes the knee
clinical: Tennis leg: tear at the musculotendinous junction of the medial head, causing sudden calf pain.
The ankle (Achilles) reflex tests the S1 root.
tus: Its two heads form the lower boundaries of the popliteal fossa.

entries.summary: A flat, broad calf muscle deep to gastrocnemius; it works continuously in standing posture.
facts: Head and upper posterior surface of the fibula, soleal line of the tibia and tendinous arch of soleus
Calcaneal tuberosity via the calcaneal tendon
Sural, posterior tibial and fibular arteries
Plantarflexes the foot (dominant with the knee bent); prevents falling forwards when standing
tus: It is the main muscle of the calf muscle pump (the 'peripheral heart') that pumps blood in the deep veins back to the heart; its venous sinuses are prone to deep vein thrombosis.

entries.summary: A flat muscle on the dorsum of the foot, palpable in front of the sinus tarsi.
facts: Upper lateral surface of the calcaneus (in front of the sinus tarsi) and inferior extensor retinaculum
Lateral sides of the long extensor tendons to toes 2–4
tus: It is one of the two muscles on the dorsum of the foot, both supplied by the deep fibular nerve. It may waste in L5 radiculopathy.

entries.summary: The most medial part of extensor digitorum brevis; a short muscle going to the big toe.
facts: Upper lateral surface of the calcaneus
Dorsal surface of the base of the proximal phalanx of the big toe
Extends the big toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint
tus: The dorsalis pedis pulse is felt lateral to the EHL tendon; the EHB tendon crosses the artery.

entries.summary: The most medial muscle of the 1st layer, running along the medial border of the sole; it supports the medial longitudinal arch.
facts: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity, flexor retinaculum and plantar aponeurosis
Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the big toe
Abducts and flexes the big toe; supports the medial arch
tus: The medial and lateral plantar nerves leaving the tarsal tunnel pass deep to this muscle; it can compress the nerves in tarsal tunnel syndrome.

entries.summary: A muscle in the middle of the 1st layer just beneath the plantar aponeurosis; its tendons split to let the long flexor tendons through.
facts: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and plantar aponeurosis
Both sides of the bases of the middle phalanges of toes 2–5
Flexes toes 2–5 at the proximal interphalangeal joint
tus: It is the foot's counterpart of the superficial finger flexor of the hand (perforatus).

entries.summary: The most lateral muscle of the 1st layer, running along the lateral border of the sole.
facts: Medial and lateral processes of the calcaneal tuberosity, plantar aponeurosis
Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the 5th toe
Abducts and flexes the little toe; supports the lateral arch
tus: Baxter's nerve (first branch of the lateral plantar nerve), implicated in heel pain, supplies this muscle.

entries.summary: A two-headed muscle in the 2nd layer of the sole that attaches to the tendon of flexor digitorum longus.
facts: Medial and lateral borders of the inferior surface of the calcaneus (two heads)
Lateral border of the flexor digitorum longus tendon
Corrects the oblique pull of the long flexor and so assists toe flexion

entries.summary: Four small muscles in the 2nd layer of the sole arising from the tendons of flexor digitorum longus.
facts: Tendons of flexor digitorum longus (1st: single head; 2nd–4th: two heads from adjacent tendons)
Medial borders of the dorsal aponeuroses of toes 2–5
1st lumbrical: medial plantar nerve; 2nd–4th lumbricals: lateral plantar nerve
Lateral plantar artery, deep plantar arch
Flex the metatarsophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints
tus: The nerve pattern resembles the hand: the first lumbrical from the medial plantar nerve (median in the hand), the others from the lateral plantar nerve (ulnar in the hand).

entries.summary: A muscle of the 3rd layer of the sole whose two heads attach to the sesamoid bones of the big toe.
facts: Plantar surfaces of the cuboid and lateral cuneiform
Both sides of the base of the proximal phalanx of the big toe (via the two sesamoid bones)
Flexes the big toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint
tus: The tendon of the long flexor of the big toe passes between its two heads, in the groove between the sesamoids.
models: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

entries.summary: A muscle of the 3rd layer of the sole with oblique and transverse heads.
facts: Oblique head: bases of metatarsals 2–4; transverse head: ligaments of the 3rd–5th metatarsophalangeal joints
Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the big toe (lateral sesamoid)
Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
Lateral plantar artery, deep plantar arch
Adducts the big toe; supports the transverse arch
clinical: In the development of hallux valgus, the pull of adductor hallucis increases the outward deviation of the big toe.

entries.en: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot
entries.summary: A small muscle of the 3rd layer of the sole running beneath the 5th metatarsal.
facts: Base of the 5th metatarsal and sheath of the fibularis longus tendon
Base of the proximal phalanx of the 5th toe
Superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
Flexes the little toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint

entries.summary: Four two-headed muscles between the metatarsals; in the foot the axis is the 2nd toe.
facts: Facing surfaces of two adjacent metatarsals (two heads)
Bases of the proximal phalanges: both sides of the 2nd toe, lateral sides of the 3rd and 4th toes
Deep plantar arch, dorsal metatarsal arteries
Abduct the toes from the axis of the 2nd toe (DAB); MTP flexion
tus: In the hand the axis of abduction is the 3rd finger, in the foot the 2nd toe.

entries.summary: Three single-headed muscles beneath metatarsals 3–5, in the deepest (4th) layer of the sole.
facts: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the same toe
Deep plantar arch, plantar metatarsal arteries
